items.stem: A coastal distress flare mortar fires a flare vertically upward at +22 m s⁻¹. Defining upward as the positive axis with g = 9.81 m s⁻² and negligible air drag, analyse the motion at t = 1.4 s. What is the vertical displacement of the object relative to the launch point at t = 1.4 s?
items.workedSolution: With upward positive, u = +22 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻². Vertical displacement s = ut + ½at² = (22)(1.4) − 0.5(9.81)(1.4)² = 21.2 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses s = ut − ½gt² with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 21.2 m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 1/2 in the gravitational displacement term −½gt².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the motion as release from rest and omits the upward initial-velocity term ut.

items.stem: In a cleanroom air-bearing guideway, a 12 kg wafer carrier moving initially at 2 m s⁻¹ is pulled for 8 s by a tether of constant tension 24 N inclined at 36.87° to the horizontal track. What is the horizontal speed at the end of the 8 s interval?
items.workedSolution: Horizontal component F_x = 24 cos(36.87°) = 19.200000000000003 N ⇒ a_x = 1.6 m s⁻². Final speed v = u + a_x t = 2 + (1.6)(8) = 14.8 m s⁻¹.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the velocity change Δv = a_x t and forgets to add the initial speed u.

items.stem: A cylindrical constantan wire of diameter 0.400 mm, length 4.50 m, and resistivity 4.90 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m is uniformly redrawn at constant volume so its new diameter is halved (0.200 mm). What is the new electrical resistance of the wire?
items.workedSolution: Initial area A = πd²/4 = 1.257 × 10⁻⁷ m² and R = ρL/A = 17.55 Ω. Scaling diameter by factor k = 0.5 scales area by k² and length by 1/k² at constant volume, so R₂ = R / k⁴ = 280.7 Ω ≈ 281 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 281 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Only scaled area by k² and forgot that constant volume also changes length by 1/k².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumed resistance varies inversely with diameter rather than diameter to the fourth power.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted the scaling factor k⁴ when computing the redrawn resistance.

items.stem: A high-resistance digital voltmeter connected across an open-circuit automotive auxiliary battery reads 12.0 V. When a 15.0 Ω resistor is connected across the terminals, the voltmeter reading drops to 10.8 V. If the 15.0 Ω resistor is replaced by a 5.00 Ω resistor, what is the new terminal potential difference?
items.workedSolution: Open-circuit reading gives ε = 12.0 V. With R₁ = 15 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 0.7200 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.667 Ω. With R₂ = 5 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 9.000 V ≈ 9.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 1.67 Ω and computes V₂ = 9.00 V.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: A rectangular cuboid ingot for an electronics heatsink cast block is machined from silver-aluminium contact alloy measuring 6 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm. markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 0.699 kg.

options.label: A

items.stem: A solid cast steel ballast block (density 7870 kg m⁻³) of mass 7.5 kg is suspended from a calibrated spring balance and lowered until it is completely submerged in freshwater of density 1000 kg m⁻³ without touching the tank floor (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) the upward buoyancy force equals the weight of fluid displaced by the body. (b) V = 9.530 × 10⁻⁴ m³ ⇒ F_B = 9.349 N ≈ 9.35 N. (c) W_app = W − F_B = 64.23 N ≈ 64.2 N.

items.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor is charged to a higher potential difference without exceeding its breakdown rating. What happens to its capacitance?
items.workedSolution: Both Q and V scale proportionally, so capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage. Verified key statement: capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.

options.label: A
options.text: Its capacitance stays constant because charge stored stays fixed as voltage increases
options.distractorRationale: Charge increases proportionally with voltage (Q = CV) so the ratio Q/V stays constant.

options.label: B
options.text: Its capacitance doubles because doubling potential difference doubles the farad rating
options.distractorRationale: Capacitance is fixed by plate geometry and dielectric, not applied voltage.

options.label: C
options.text: Its capacitance stays constant because capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage

options.label: D
options.text: Its capacitance halves because potential difference appears in the denominator of charge per volt
options.distractorRationale: Forgets that Q also doubles when V doubles, keeping C = Q/V invariant.

items.stem: A student takes repeated measurements of wire diameter using a micrometer whose zero mark does not align cleanly when closed.
items.workedSolution: (a) random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging. (b) averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error. Core principle: repeat averaging reduces random scatter while calibration removes systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to repeat averaging reduces random scatter while calibration removes systematic offset.
States primary causal step: averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (systematic errors such as zero offset bias every measurement consistently in the same direction).

items.stem: A charged capacitor discharges through a fixed resistor. The experiment is repeated from the same initial voltage after replacing the resistor with one of smaller resistance. Without calculation, how does the discharge change?
items.workedSolution: From τ = RC and I = V/R, a smaller resistance reduces the time constant so initial current is larger and capacitor potential difference falls more rapidly. Verified key statement: smaller resistance reduces the time constant so initial current is larger and capacitor potential difference falls more rapidly.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that smaller resistance reduces the time constant so initial current is larger and capacitor potential difference falls more rapidly.

options.label: A
options.text: A smaller resistance increases the time constant so initial current drops and voltage stays higher for longer
options.distractorRationale: Time constant τ = R C decreases, not increases, when R is reduced.

options.label: B
options.text: A smaller resistance reduces the time constant so initial current is larger and capacitor potential difference falls more rapidly

options.label: C
options.text: A smaller resistance keeps the time constant unchanged because capacitance alone controls discharge speed
options.distractorRationale: Time constant depends on the product of BOTH resistance and capacitance.

options.label: D
options.text: A smaller resistance reduces initial current while doubling the total charge initially stored on the plates
options.distractorRationale: Initial charge Q = C V depends only on capacitance and initial voltage, not the discharge resistor.

items.stem: A dense sphere is released from rest at the top of a deep tank filled with viscous oil.
items.workedSolution: (a) initially weight exceeds drag so the object accelerates downward and speed increases. (b) drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero. Core principle: balance between speed dependent drag and constant weight yields zero acceleration.

markScheme.criterion: States accurately that initially weight exceeds drag so the object accelerates downward and speed increases.
First causal step: initially weight exceeds drag so the object accelerates downward and speed increases.
Intermediate physical mechanism: resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration.
Final physical conclusion: when upward drag equals downward weight resultant force becomes zero so velocity stays constant at terminal velocity.

items.stem: When illuminated smoke trapped in a glass cell is observed through a microscope, bright specks dance along erratic zig-zag paths. What causes this motion?
items.workedSolution: Brownian motion arises because uneven rapid collisions from much smaller invisible randomly moving air molecules transfer momentum to smoke specks. Verified key statement: uneven rapid collisions from much smaller invisible randomly moving air molecules transfer momentum to smoke specks.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that uneven rapid collisions from much smaller invisible randomly moving air molecules transfer momentum to smoke specks.

options.label: A
options.text: It occurs because visible air molecules collide directly with one another under the microscope lamp
options.distractorRationale: Air molecules are far too small to be seen under an optical microscope; only smoke specks are visible.

options.label: B
options.text: It occurs because uneven rapid collisions from much smaller invisible randomly moving air molecules transfer momentum to smoke specks

options.label: C
options.text: It occurs because steady upward convection currents sweep all specks smoothly in one direction
options.distractorRationale: Convection produces smooth collective drift, not random individual zig-zag jitter.

options.label: D
options.text: It occurs because the microscope lamp pushes the specks randomly with intense radiation pressure
options.distractorRationale: Radiation pressure from a bench lamp is negligible and directional rather than randomly fluctuating.

items.stem: Which statement accurately expresses Lenz's law of electromagnetic induction?
items.workedSolution: Lenz's law states that the direction of induced electromotive force opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it. Verified key statement: direction of induced electromotive force opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that direction of induced electromotive force opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it.

options.label: A
options.text: The direction of induced electromotive force opposes the change in magnetic flux linkage producing it

options.label: B
options.text: The magnitude of induced electromotive force is always equal to the steady magnetic flux through the coil
options.distractorRationale: Confuses Faraday's rate-of-change law with steady flux and omits direction.

options.label: C
options.text: The direction of induced current always assists the motion of the magnet to conserve charge
options.distractorRationale: Assisting motion would create energy from nothing, violating conservation of energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The induced current always flows clockwise regardless of magnet polarity
options.distractorRationale: Induced current direction reverses whenever magnet polarity or direction of motion reverses.

items.stem: Which defining condition must an oscillating mass satisfy to execute simple harmonic motion?
items.workedSolution: In simple harmonic motion, acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from a fixed equilibrium position and always directed toward it. Verified key statement: acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from a fixed equilibrium position and always directed toward it.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from a fixed equilibrium position and always directed toward it.

options.label: A
options.text: Its velocity is directly proportional to displacement and directed away from equilibrium
options.distractorRationale: Velocity is maximum at equilibrium and zero at turning points, not proportional to displacement.

options.label: B
options.text: Its acceleration stays constant in magnitude and reverses sign only at the endpoints
options.distractorRationale: Constant acceleration produces parabolic motion, not sinusoidal simple harmonic motion.

options.label: C
options.text: Its periodic oscillation repeats with constant amplitude regardless of force law
options.distractorRationale: Not every periodic motion is simple harmonic; acceleration must be proportional and opposite to displacement.

options.label: D

items.stem: By dimensional homogeneity, the transverse wave speed v along a taut cable depends only on tension T (in N, i.e. kg m s⁻²) and linear mass density μ (mass per unit length) via v = Tᵃ μᵇ with dimensionless constant equal to unity. In an acoustic wire rig, T = 48 N ± 1.2 N and μ = 3 g m⁻¹ ± 0.1 g m⁻¹. Deduce the exponents a and b by dimensional homogeneity and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Matching SI base units: [v] = m s⁻¹, [T] = kg m s⁻², [μ] = kg m⁻¹. For kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, −2a = −1 ⇒ a = 0.5 and b = −0.5, so v = √(T/μ). With μ = 3 × 10⁻³ = 0.003 kg m⁻¹, v = √(48 / 0.003) = 126 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a = 1/2, b = −1/2, converts μ to 0.003 kg m⁻¹, and obtains v = 126 m s⁻¹.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Deduces v = √(T/μ) correctly but forgets to convert μ from g m⁻¹ into kg m⁻¹ (off by √1000).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a = 1, b = −1 (computing T/μ with units m² s⁻²) without taking the square root required by dimensional homogeneity.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the dimensional ratio to √(μ/T), yielding s m⁻¹ instead of m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A wind-turbine hub sensor test rotates an accelerometer pod at speed 9 m s⁻¹ ± 0.2 m s⁻¹ around a circle of radius 4 m ± 0.03 m, where a = v² / r. What is the percentage uncertainty in the calculated centripetal acceleration a?
items.workedSolution: For a = v² / r, Δa/a = 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) = 2(0.2/9) + (0.03/4). Multiplying by 100% gives 5.19%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses %Δa = 2(%Δv) + (%Δr) to obtain 5.19%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 on the fractional uncertainty of v despite v being squared in v²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainty of r from 2(%Δv) because r is in the denominator.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the percentage uncertainties instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: A prestressing tendon strand filament with circular diameter d = 0.8 mm ± 0.01 mm is tensioned to F = 135 N ± 0.5 N in a calibration frame. What is the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = π(0.8 × 10⁻³)² / 4 = 5.03 × 10⁻⁷ m². Tensile stress σ = F / A = 4F / (πd²) = 2.69 × 10⁸ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 in m² to obtain σ = 2.69 × 10⁸ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses A = πd² instead of A = πd²/4 (treating diameter d as if it were radius r, off by a factor of 4).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter in millimetres directly without converting d² from mm² to 10⁻⁶ m².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by circumference πd instead of cross-sectional area πd²/4.

items.stem: Consider a hydroelectric reservoir concrete floor valve, which has a flat horizontal surface of area 2 m² situated at a depth of 28.5 m beneath the open surface of freshwater of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Take atmospheric pressure at the free surface as 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the total downward force exerted by the fluid and atmosphere on this surface?
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1000 × 9.81 × 28.5 = 2.796 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 2.80 × 10⁵ Pa. Absolute pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 2.796 × 10⁵ = 3.806 × 10⁵ Pa = 380.6 kPa ≈ 381 kPa. Total force F = p_abs A = 3.806 × 10⁵ × 2 = 7.612 × 10⁵ N ≈ 7.61 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 7.61 × 10⁵ N.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides absolute pressure by area instead of multiplying F = p A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure, omitting atmospheric force.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes fluid mass instead of total downward force.

items.stem: Two equal and opposite parallel forces act at opposite ends of a steering wheel (a couple). The resultant force is zero, yet the wheel is NOT in equilibrium. Why?
items.workedSolution: Complete rigid body equilibrium also requires zero resultant force in any direction alongside zero resultant moment about any point. Verified key statement: complete rigid body equilibrium also requires zero resultant force in any direction.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that complete rigid body equilibrium also requires zero resultant force in any direction.

options.label: A
options.text: Because equilibrium only requires resultant force to be zero and never depends on turning moments
options.distractorRationale: A couple has zero resultant force yet produces a net turning torque.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the two forces must act in the same direction to establish static equilibrium
options.distractorRationale: Same-direction forces yield a non-zero resultant force and accelerate the centre of mass.

options.label: C
options.text: Because complete rigid body equilibrium also requires zero resultant force in any direction

options.label: D
options.text: Because rigid body equilibrium requires both resultant force and resultant moment to be non zero
options.distractorRationale: Equilibrium requires both resultant force and resultant moment to be ZERO.

items.stem: Before thermal cycling, an aerospace ceramic insulator cube is logged with side length 4.5 cm ± 0.03 cm and mass 656 g ± 4 g. What is the absolute uncertainty Δρ in the density when expressed in kg m⁻³?
items.workedSolution: First find ρ = (0.656) / (0.045)³ = 7.20 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Fractional uncertainty Δρ/ρ = (4/656) + 3(0.03/4.5) = 0.0261. Therefore Δρ = ρ × (Δρ/ρ) = 188 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Combines SI density with fractional uncertainty Δm/m + 3ΔL/L to obtain Δρ = 188 kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 3 from L³ when propagating the fractional uncertainty of the edge length.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the absolute uncertainty in g cm⁻³ rather than converting to kg m⁻³.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the fractional uncertainty of L³ from that of mass in the quotient m / L³.

items.stem: A pure crystalline wax sample is heated steadily by an electrical heater. During melting, the thermometer reading stays flat on a horizontal plateau. What happens at the molecular scale during this plateau?
items.workedSolution: During melting, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while supplied energy increases internal potential energy by breaking bonds. Verified key statement: mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while supplied energy increases internal potential energy by breaking bonds.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while supplied energy increases internal potential energy by breaking bonds.

options.label: A
options.text: Along the plateau, both molecular kinetic energy and molecular potential energy remain completely constant
options.distractorRationale: Energy is continually supplied by the heater, so internal potential energy must increase.

options.label: B
options.text: Along the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy rises steadily while molecular potential energy decreases
options.distractorRationale: A rise in mean molecular kinetic energy would raise the temperature rather than keeping a plateau.

options.label: C
options.text: Along the plateau, all heater energy escapes immediately into the room so internal energy cannot change
options.distractorRationale: Even with negligible heat loss, melting requires latent heat to weaken intermolecular bonds.

options.label: D
options.text: Along the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while supplied energy increases internal potential energy by breaking bonds

items.stem: Which statement gives the exact form of the Pressure Law for an ideal gas?
items.workedSolution: The Pressure Law states that for a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin. Verified key statement: for a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that for a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin.

options.label: A
options.text: It states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to temperature in degrees Celsius
options.distractorRationale: Pressure vs Celsius has a non-zero intercept at freezing point; direct proportionality requires kelvin.

options.label: B
options.text: It states that for a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin

options.label: C
options.text: It states that for any mass of gas at constant pressure volume is inversely proportional to kelvin temperature
options.distractorRationale: Mixes up Charles's law variables and inverts proportionality.

options.label: D
options.text: It states that pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature regardless of vessel expansion
options.distractorRationale: Omits the controlled variable of constant volume.

items.stem: During a steady-state dyno road-load run at 36 km h⁻¹, an electric drivetrain overcomes 800 N of resistive force while drawing 9524 W of DC electrical power for 40 s. What is the percentage efficiency of the propulsion drivetrain?
items.workedSolution: At constant velocity, tractive force F = 800 N and v = 36/3.6 = 10 m s⁻¹. Useful power P_out = Fv = 800 × 10 = 8000 W. Efficiency η = (8000/9524) × 100% = 84.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Converts speed to 10 m s⁻¹, computes P_out = Fv = 8000 W, and obtains η = 84.0%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies drag force in N by speed in km h⁻¹ without dividing speed by 3.6 to obtain watts.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical power dissipated as heat rather than drivetrain efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by velocity (F/v) instead of multiplying P = Fv.

Obtains v = 27.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The universal NAND-only network shown ties both inputs of the first NAND gate to A, ties both inputs of the second NAND gate to B, and feeds their outputs D and E into a third NAND gate. What single gate function does this three-NAND arrangement synthesise?
items.workedSolution: Each tied NAND acts as an inverter ($D = \bar{A}$, $E = \bar{B}$). The output NAND computes $Q = \overline{\bar{A} \cdot \bar{B}} = \overline{\bar{A}} + \overline{\bar{B}} = A + B$, a single two-input OR gate.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that single two-input OR gate.

items.stem: A heating element is made from a uniform cylindrical alloy resistance wire of diameter 0.220 mm, length 4.20 m, and resistivity 9.50 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. It is connected across a steady 48.0 V DC supply.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates A = πd²/4 = 3.80 × 10⁻⁸ m² and substitutes into R = ρL/A.
Correct resistance 105 Ω.
Correct power P = V²/R = 22.0 W.
Computes conserved volume V = AL = 1.60 × 10⁻⁷ m³ and sets s³ = V.
Correct cube edge length 5.42 mm.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical resistance of the wire.
Calculate the thermal power output of the heating element at 48.0 V.
The wire is later melted down without loss and cast into a solid cube. Calculate the edge length of the cube in mm.
workingSteps: Volume conserved: V = AL = 3.801 × 10⁻⁸ m² × 4.2 = 1.597 × 10⁻⁷ m³.

items.stem: On a crash-attenuator sled track, a 0.06 kg buffer module travelling at +18 m s⁻¹ impacts an elastomeric stop for 12.5 ms and rebounds in the reverse direction at speed 16 m s⁻¹. What is the signed change in kinetic energy ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i during the impact?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ½m(v² − u²) including negative sign to obtain -2.04 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes positive energy lost (E_k,i − E_k,f) instead of the signed change E_k,f − E_k,i.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates ½m(v − u)² instead of ½mv² − ½mu².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds the two kinetic energies because the velocity reversed sign, forgetting v² is always positive.

items.stem: An ideal voltmeter placed directly across the terminals of a four-cell rechargeable pack on open circuit reads 4.80 V. When a 6.00 Ω load resistor is connected across the battery, the voltmeter reading falls to 4.00 V. The first load is then removed and replaced by a 2.40 Ω load resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 0.667 A and substitutes into r = (ε − V₁) / I₁.
Correct internal resistance 1.20 Ω.
Uses V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) (or finds I₂ then I₂R₂).
Correct terminal potential difference 3.20 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.
workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 4 / 6 = 0.6667 A.
Internal resistance r = (ε − V₁) / I₁ = (4.8 − 4) / 0.6667 A = 1.200 Ω ≈ 1.20 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new terminal potential difference across the 2.40 Ω resistor.
workingSteps: Terminal pd V₂ = I₂ R₂ = 1.333 A × 2.4 = 3.200 V ≈ 3.20 V.

items.stem: An electroplating bath connected across a 4.50 V supply draws a constant current of 1.45 A for 8 min. How many electrons pass a fixed cross-section of the connecting wire in this time?
items.workedSolution: Convert time t = 8 × 60 = 480 s and current I = 1.450 A. Total charge Q = It = 696.0 C. Number of electrons N = Q / e = 696.0 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 4.350 × 10²¹ ≈ 4.35 × 10²¹.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 4.35 × 10²¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert time from minutes to seconds (factor of 60 error).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applied the wrong unit conversion factor for current or time.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied charge by e instead of dividing Q by e.

items.stem: A biomechanics lab tests a carbon-composite leaf spring: optical ruler readings shift from x₁ = 15 mm ± 1 mm at zero load to x₂ = 95 mm ± 1 mm under tension F = 60 N ± 0.6 N. Using Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx₁ + Δx₂, what is the percentage uncertainty in the spring constant k = F / (x₂ − x₁)?
items.workedSolution: Extension e = x₂ − x₁ = 95 − 15 = 80 mm with absolute uncertainty Δe = Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 1 + 1 = 2 mm. Thus %Δk = (%ΔF) + (%Δe) = (0.6/60 + 2/80) × 100% = 3.50%.

markScheme.criterion: Finds e = 80 mm, Δe = 2 mm, and obtains %Δk = 3.50%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the uncertainty of a single ruler reading Δx rather than summing Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 2Δx for the difference x₂ − x₁.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumes Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx − Δx = 0 by subtracting absolute uncertainties in a difference.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the fractional uncertainty of extension from %ΔF in the quotient F / e.

items.stem: A wave-basin carriage drive draws 2813 W electrically while towing a hydrofoil rig horizontally at 6 m s⁻¹ for 50 s by a line of tension 600 N held at 60° to the motion. How much energy is wasted to the surroundings over the 50 s interval?
items.workedSolution: Useful power P_out = Fv cos(60°) = 1800 W. Wasted power = 2813 − 1800 = 1013 W. Over 50 s, E_wasted = (1013)(50) = 5.07 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts Fv cos 60° from 2813 W and multiplies by 50 s to get 5.07 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes wasted power in watts (P_in − P_out) and forgets to multiply by the time interval.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the useful mechanical work done Fvt cos θ instead of the wasted energy.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to resolve cable tension by cos θ before subtracting from input power.

items.stem: A rectangular micro-machined resistor bar has length 32 mm, width 0.9 mm, and height 0.35 mm. A potential difference of 6.00 V is applied across its two 0.9 mm × 0.35 mm end faces, where its resistance is measured to be 2.23 Ω.

Correct value 2.20 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m.
Substitutes V and R into P = V² / R.
Correct power dissipated 16.1 W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the cross-sectional area perpendicular to current flow and hence determine the resistivity of the material.
Calculate the electrical power dissipated in the bar at this potential difference.

items.stem: A warming tray heater is rated "230 V, 460 W" and is operated continuously at its rated voltage for 4 min.

items.stem: During a biomedical materials test, a nickel-titanium alloy wire of gauge length 3 m and cross-section 1.2 mm² elongates by 1.8 mm under axial force 201.6 N, with ±3% stress uncertainty and ±2.5% strain uncertainty. What is the Young modulus E of the wire in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Tensile stress σ = F / A = 201.6 / (1.2 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.68 × 10⁸ Pa. Tensile strain ε = ΔL / L = (1.8 × 10⁻³) / 3 = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴. Young modulus E = σ / ε = 2.80 × 10¹¹ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates σ = F/A and ε = ΔL/L in SI units to obtain E = 2.80 × 10¹¹ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Converts mm² to m² using 10⁻³ instead of (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁶, underestimating stress and Young modulus by 10³.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets both mm² → 10⁻⁶ m² and mm → 10⁻³ m unit prefix powers properly.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies tensile stress by tensile strain (σ × ε) instead of dividing σ / ε.

items.stem: A semiconductor light-emitting diode is tested across both forward and reverse bias using a variable DC source.
items.workedSolution: (a) resistance is extremely high in reverse bias and below the forward threshold voltage so current is virtually zero. (b) a protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction. Core principle: asymmetric threshold conduction defines a semiconductor diode characteristic.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: resistance is extremely high in reverse bias and below the forward threshold voltage so current is virtually zero.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to asymmetric threshold conduction defines a semiconductor diode characteristic.
States primary causal step: a protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (above the forward threshold potential difference resistance falls sharply and current rises rapidly).

parts.prompt: Describe the key regions of the current against potential difference sketch graph in reverse bias and in forward bias. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: resistance is extremely high in reverse bias and below the forward threshold voltage so current is virtually zero.
workingSteps: Establish the core NCUK mark point: resistance is extremely high in reverse bias and below the forward threshold voltage so current is virtually zero.
Anchor concept: asymmetric threshold conduction defines a semiconductor diode characteristic.

parts.prompt: Explain what happens above the forward threshold potential difference and why a protective series resistor is required. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: a protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction.
workingSteps: Develop the causal explanation clearly without algebraic shortcuts: a protective series resistor is included to limit current and prevent thermal damage to the junction.
Avoid the common error of expecting a symmetrical curve through the origin in both forward and reverse bias.

items.stem: In a precision galvanometer coil, a uniform cylindrical high-purity silver wire of diameter 0.800 mm carries a steady current of 2.40 A. The free-electron number density in the high-purity silver is 5.80 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the mean drift speed of the conduction electrons.
items.workedSolution: Convert diameter to metres: d = 8.000 × 10⁻⁴ m. Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = 5.027 × 10⁻⁷ m². Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives v = I / (nAe) = 5.145 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 5.15 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 5.15 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied by 4 instead of dividing by 4 in A = πd²/4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π when calculating the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: A solid billet of oxygen-free copper with mass 0.8 kg and density 8930 kg m⁻³ is drawn without material loss into a uniform cylindrical wire of diameter 0.8 mm (or alternatively melted and cast into a solid cube). What is the total length of the drawn cylindrical wire in m?

items.stem: Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², a pumped-storage auxiliary pump consuming 10889 W raises 400 kg of water vertically through a head of 30 m in 15 s at constant flow speed. How much energy is wasted during the 15 s lift?

items.stem: A rectangular cuboid ingot for a motorsport piston-blank casting is machined from titanium-copper brazing alloy measuring 12 cm × 5 cm × 4.5 cm. The alloy is composed of 30% copper (density 8930 kg m⁻³) and 70% titanium (density 4510 kg m⁻³) by volume.

items.stem: An electric immersion heater rated at 144 W is switched on for 100 s inside a 0.4 kg sample of silicone heat-transfer oil (specific heat capacity c = 1800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), raising its uniform temperature by 15 K. items.stem: A solid machined titanium ballast block (density 4510 kg m⁻³) of mass 22.5 kg is suspended from a calibrated spring balance and lowered until it is completely submerged in freshwater of density 1000 kg m⁻³ without touching the tank floor (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). items.workedSolution: Block volume V = m / ρ_obj = 22.5 / 4510 = 4.989 × 10⁻³ m³. Upthrust F_B = ρ_fluid V g = 1000 × 4.989 × 10⁻³ × 9.81 = 48.94 N ≈ 48.9 N. Apparent weight W_app = m g − F_B = 220.7 − 48.94 = 171.8 N ≈ 172 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value = 172 N.

options.distractorRationale: Reports weight in air, ignoring buoyancy.

options.label: C

options.label: D

items.stem: Using typical everyday physical dimensions and water density $\rho \approx 1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}$, estimate the order of magnitude of the mass of a single spherical raindrop.

Option D (1.00 × 10⁻⁵ kg) matches.

items.stem: Which statement gives the full definition of Young's modulus for a solid material?
items.workedSolution: Young's modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the linear elastic region. Verified key statement: ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the linear elastic region.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the linear elastic region.

options.label: A
options.text: It is the ratio of applied load to extension for a specific wire sample
options.distractorRationale: Defines the spring constant k = F / x (geometry dependent), not the material constant Young modulus.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the ratio of tensile strain to tensile stress across the plastic region
options.distractorRationale: Inverts stress over strain and uses the plastic region instead of the linear elastic region.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the maximum tensile stress a specimen can sustain before breaking
options.distractorRationale: Defines ultimate tensile strength rather than Young's modulus.

options.label: D
options.text: It is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the linear elastic region

items.stem: Two wires made of the same copper alloy have different lengths and diameters at the same laboratory temperature.
items.workedSolution: (a) resistance of a specimen of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) material property independent of sample dimensions at constant temperature. Core principle: resistivity depends on the material and temperature rather than wire geometry.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: resistance of a specimen of unit length and unit cross sectional area.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to resistivity depends on the material and temperature rather than wire geometry.
States primary causal step: material property independent of sample dimensions at constant temperature.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (material property independent of sample dimensions at constant temperature).

parts.expectedAnswer: resistance of a specimen of unit length and unit cross sectional area.

items.stem: Which pair of derived SI unit expressions are both equivalent to the volt?
items.workedSolution: Potential difference is work done per unit charge (V = W / Q), so one volt equals joule per coulomb and newton metre per coulomb (J C⁻¹ = N m C⁻¹ = J A⁻¹ s⁻¹). Verified key statement: joule per coulomb and newton metre per coulomb.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that joule per coulomb and newton metre per coulomb.

options.label: A
options.text: Both newton per coulomb and joule coulomb (N C⁻¹ and J C)
options.distractorRationale: Confuses electric field strength (N C⁻¹) and multiplied work-charge (J C) with potential difference.

options.label: B
options.text: Both joule per coulomb and newton metre per coulomb (J C⁻¹ and N m C⁻¹)

options.label: C
options.text: Both coulomb per joule and watt ampere (C J⁻¹ and W A)
options.distractorRationale: Inverts energy per unit charge and multiplies power by current instead of dividing.

options.label: D
options.text: Both joule per second and ampere second (J s⁻¹ and A s)
options.distractorRationale: Lists units for electrical power (watt) and charge (coulomb) rather than potential difference.

items.stem: Why does replacing a low-resistance analogue voltmeter with a high-resistance digital voltmeter improve accuracy across a large resistor in a potential divider?
items.workedSolution: Ideally, infinite internal resistance ensures negligible current is diverted through the voltmeter so the divider ratio stays unperturbed. Verified key statement: infinite internal resistance ensures negligible current is diverted through the voltmeter.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that infinite internal resistance ensures negligible current is diverted through the voltmeter.

options.label: A
options.text: Because lower internal resistance allows extra current to boost the voltmeter coil deflection
options.distractorRationale: Extra meter current loads the divider and depresses the measured potential difference.

options.label: B
options.text: Because infinite resistance increases the electromotive force supplied by the power pack
options.distractorRationale: A voltmeter cannot alter the chemical electromotive force of the power supply.

options.label: C
options.text: Because higher meter resistance eliminates the internal resistance of the DC power pack
options.distractorRationale: The source internal resistance is fixed inside the supply regardless of the voltmeter.

options.label: D
options.text: Because infinite internal resistance ensures negligible current is diverted through the voltmeter

items.stem: When an open-circuit battery is connected to a headlamp bulb, the voltmeter reading across its terminals drops noticeably.
items.workedSolution: (a) electromotive force transfers energy to charge in a source whereas potential difference transfers electrical energy from charge to components. (b) internal resistance dissipates energy inside the source causing lost volts so terminal potential difference falls below electromotive force under load. Core principle: direction of energy conversion distinguishes a source from a load.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: electromotive force transfers energy to charge in a source whereas potential difference transfers electrical energy from charge to components.

Completes full physical linkage without misconception (potential difference is electrical energy transferred into thermal or other forms per unit charge across a component).

items.stem: A negative temperature coefficient thermistor is wired in series with a fixed resistor across a constant-voltage battery. Without calculation, what happens when the thermistor is warmed in hot water?
items.workedSolution: In an NTC thermistor divider, heating releases more charge carriers lowering thermistor resistance so its share of potential difference falls while the fixed resistor voltage rises. Verified key statement: heating releases more charge carriers lowering thermistor resistance so its share of potential difference falls while the fixed resistor voltage rises.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that heating releases more charge carriers lowering thermistor resistance so its share of potential difference falls while the fixed resistor voltage rises.

options.label: A
options.text: As temperature increases, lattice vibration raises thermistor resistance so the fixed resistor receives a smaller voltage share
options.distractorRationale: Confuses a semiconductor NTC thermistor with a metal filament lamp.

options.label: B
options.text: As temperature increases, thermistor resistance drops to zero while total circuit current decreases
options.distractorRationale: Lowering series resistance increases, rather than decreases, circuit current.

options.label: C
options.text: As temperature increases, heating releases more charge carriers lowering thermistor resistance so its share of potential difference falls while the fixed resistor voltage rises

options.label: D
options.text: As temperature increases, potential difference across both the thermistor and fixed resistor increases simultaneously
options.distractorRationale: The two potential differences must sum to the constant battery electromotive force.

items.stem: An oscilloscope displays eight tightly packed sinusoidal cycles across the screen. How should the student adjust the time-base to improve precision in measuring the period, and what happens if the time-base is switched off completely?
items.workedSolution: Correct experimental practice: Reduce the time base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty and switching time base off produces a vertical line of height peak to peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Reduce the time base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty and switching time base off produces a vertical line of height peak to peak voltage.

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce the time base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty and switching time base off produces a vertical line of height peak to peak voltage.

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the time-base setting to pack more cycles onto the screen, while switching time-base off turns the trace into a single stationary dot.
options.distractorRationale: Increasing ms div⁻¹ compresses cycles further; an AC signal with time-base off produces a vertical line of height V_pp (only DC makes a dot).

options.label: C
options.text: Increase Y-gain to stretch the trace horizontally, while switching time-base off displays a horizontal line at V_rms.
options.distractorRationale: Y-gain scales vertical voltage, not horizontal time; time-base off collapses horizontal sweep to zero.

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce Y-gain to expand the horizontal period and switching time-base off clears the screen completely.
options.distractorRationale: Time-base controls horizontal sweep; with sweep off the electron beam oscillates vertically across V_pp.

items.stem: In both resistivity (RP5) and Young modulus (RP4) investigations, why does a student devote particular care to micrometer measurements of wire diameter $d$?

items.stem: A parallel-plate air capacitor is charged first to a low voltage and later to a higher voltage.
items.workedSolution: (a) capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. (b) capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage. Core principle: capacitance equals charge stored divided by potential difference.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to capacitance equals charge stored divided by potential difference.
States primary causal step: capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (one coulomb of charge stored when potential difference across the plates is one volt).

parts.prompt: Define the farad cleanly. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Establish the core NCUK mark point: capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
Anchor concept: capacitance equals charge stored divided by potential difference.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain whether raising the charging voltage alters the capacitance of the capacitor. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.
workingSteps: Develop the causal explanation clearly without algebraic shortcuts: capacitance of a given geometry is constant and independent of applied voltage.
Avoid the common error of defining the farad as energy stored per volt rather than charge stored per volt.

items.stem: A student repeats a timing measurement several times using a stopwatch with a constant start-delay offset. Which statement correctly compares random and systematic errors?
items.workedSolution: Random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging. Verified key statement: random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging.

options.label: A
options.text: In experimental physics, systematic errors scatter unpredictably and are eliminated by taking a large mean
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the properties of random and systematic errors; averaging cannot fix a constant offset.

options.label: B
options.text: In experimental physics, random errors scatter unpredictably and are reduced by repeating and averaging whereas systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not reduced by averaging

options.label: C
options.text: In experimental physics, both random and systematic errors are completely removed by repeating readings
options.distractorRationale: Repeating and averaging reduces random scatter only and leaves systematic bias untouched.

options.label: D
options.text: In experimental physics, random errors shift every reading by the same fixed amount in one direction
options.distractorRationale: Describes a constant systematic zero error rather than random variation.

items.stem: A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor. The resistor is then replaced by one of smaller resistance from the same initial voltage.
items.workedSolution: (a) time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant. (b) initial discharge current increases because initial voltage is divided by a smaller resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that initial discharge current increases because initial voltage is divided by a smaller resistance.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state how the circuit time constant changes. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant.
workingSteps: Identify the primary physical statement: time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, explain how the remaining capacitor voltage at a fixed later instant compares. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: initial discharge current increases because initial voltage is divided by a smaller resistance.
workingSteps: Link the physical principle (shorter time constant produces a steeper exponential decay curve) to the required condition or mechanism: initial discharge current increases because initial voltage is divided by a smaller resistance.

items.stem: A skydiver leaps from a stationary balloon and falls vertically before opening the parachute. Why does the gradient of the skydiver's velocity–time graph decrease gradually toward zero?
items.workedSolution: The gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration: resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration. Verified key statement: resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration.

options.label: A
options.text: During the fall, gravitational field strength drops rapidly toward zero as altitude decreases
options.distractorRationale: Gravity stays virtually constant over skydiving altitudes.

options.label: B
options.text: During the fall, resistive drag force grows with speed reducing the downward resultant force and acceleration

options.label: C
options.text: During the fall, air resistance stays constant while the skydiver loses mass
options.distractorRationale: Air drag grows strongly with speed while mass remains constant.

options.label: D
options.text: During the fall, upward drag decreases with speed so acceleration climbs smoothly
options.distractorRationale: Drag increases with speed, reducing acceleration.

items.stem: A small stone whirled on a string moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Which statement correctly explains its acceleration and the work done by the centripetal force?
items.workedSolution: In uniform circular motion, velocity direction changes continuously so resultant centripetal force and acceleration act perpendicular to velocity toward the centre doing zero work. Verified key statement: velocity direction changes continuously so resultant centripetal force and acceleration act perpendicular to velocity toward the centre doing zero work.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that velocity direction changes continuously so resultant centripetal force and acceleration act perpendicular to velocity toward the centre doing zero work.

options.label: A
options.text: Throughout the orbit, velocity direction changes continuously so resultant centripetal force and acceleration act perpendicular to velocity toward the centre doing zero work

options.label: B
options.text: Throughout the orbit, acceleration is zero because speed stays constant while an outward centrifugal force balances tension
options.distractorRationale: Velocity changes direction continuously so acceleration is non-zero; no outward centrifugal force acts on the stone.

options.label: C
options.text: Throughout the orbit, the centripetal force acts along the tangent and continually increases the kinetic energy
options.distractorRationale: Centripetal force points radially inward perpendicular to velocity, so speed and kinetic energy stay constant.

options.label: D
options.text: Throughout the orbit, acceleration points radially outward away from the centre while doing positive work
options.distractorRationale: Acceleration points toward the centre and perpendicular force does zero work.

items.stem: In a smoke-cell demonstration, a horizontal beam illuminates airborne smoke particles viewed from above through a microscope.
items.workedSolution: (a) bright specks undergo erratic zig zag random motion viewed under the microscope. (b) much smaller invisible air molecules moving rapidly in random directions collide unevenly with opposite sides of each speck. Core principle: unbalanced microscopic molecular impacts drive observable random speck jitter.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: bright specks undergo erratic zig zag random motion viewed under the microscope.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to unbalanced microscopic molecular impacts drive observable random speck jitter.

items.stem: A bar magnet is pushed steadily into a solenoid connected to a sensitive galvanometer.
items.workedSolution: (a) induced electromotive force or current acts in a direction that opposes the change producing it. (b) follows directly from conservation of energy because mechanical work must be done against the opposing magnetic force.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that induced electromotive force or current acts in a direction that opposes the change producing it.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that follows directly from conservation of energy because mechanical work must be done against the opposing magnetic force.

items.stem: A mass suspended from a helical spring oscillates vertically in simple harmonic motion.
items.workedSolution: (a) acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from a fixed equilibrium point. (b) acceleration is always directed opposite to displacement toward the equilibrium position.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from a fixed equilibrium point.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that acceleration is always directed opposite to displacement toward the equilibrium position.

parts.prompt: State the direction of acceleration throughout the oscillation. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: acceleration is always directed opposite to displacement toward the equilibrium position.

items.stem: A hydroelectric reservoir piezometer tube measures head depth h = 8.5 m ± 0.8 m in fluid of density ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ ± 10 kg m⁻³; take g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ as exact. What is the absolute uncertainty Δp in the hydrostatic gauge pressure in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Nominal gauge pressure p = ρgh = 8.33 × 10⁴ Pa. Fractional uncertainty Δp/p = Δρ/ρ + Δh/h = 10/1000 + 0.8/8.5 = 0.104. Hence Δp = 8.67 × 10³ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes p(Δρ/ρ + Δh/h) to obtain Δp = 8.67 × 10³ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the fractional uncertainties |Δρ/ρ − Δh/h| instead of adding them.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies absolute uncertainties Δρ × g × Δh directly instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Propagates fractional uncertainties correctly but forgets the factor of g in p = ρgh.

items.stem: Dimensional analysis of a tensioned overhead catenary wire shows that mechanical pulse speed obeys v = Tᵃ μᵇ (unit prefactor), where T is axial tension and μ is mass per unit length. Field sensors record T = 144 N ± 2.4 N on a conductor of μ = 6 g m⁻¹ ± 0.3 g m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates SI base dimensions kg, m, s to deduce a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.
Converts linear density to 0.006 kg m⁻¹ and substitutes into √(T/μ).
Obtains v = 155 m s⁻¹.
Multiplies both %ΔT and %Δμ by 1/2 before adding.
Obtains 3.33%.
Obtains Δv = 5.16 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By equating SI base units on both sides of v = Tᵃ μᵇ, determine a and b and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: [T] = kg m s⁻² and [μ] = kg m⁻¹ ⇒ kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, so a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in v.
Determine the absolute uncertainty Δv in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An aerospace human-centrifuge gondola orbits at tangential speed v = 14 m s⁻¹ ± 0.3 m s⁻¹ along a circular arm of radius r = 1.6 m ± 0.08 m, producing centripetal acceleration a = v² / r.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes v and r into a = v² / r.
Obtains a = 123 m s⁻².
Uses 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) and converts to a percentage.
Obtains 9.29%.
Obtains Δa = 11.4 m s⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the nominal centripetal acceleration a.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a.

items.stem: A surgical stainless-steel suture wire of circular cross-section has micrometer diameter d = 1.5 mm ± 0.02 mm and carries an axial tensile load F = 75 N ± 1 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 with d converted from mm to m.

Obtains Δσ = 1.70 × 10⁶ Pa.

items.stem: An atmospheric lidar calibration sphere is projected vertically upward from a tower platform with initial velocity +18 m s⁻¹. Neglecting drag and taking upward as positive with g = 9.81 m s⁻², consider its state 2.6 s later. What is the signed vertical velocity at t = 2.6 s?
items.workedSolution: Using v = u + at with u = +18 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻² gives v = 18 − (9.81)(2.6) = -7.51 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A

items.stem: A glaciology instrument sled of mass 10 kg glides along horizontal frictionless ice at initial speed 1.5 m s⁻¹ when a winch cable applies a constant tension of 24 N angled at 60° above the horizontal for 4 s (sled remains in contact with the ice). What horizontal distance does the body travel during the 4 s interval?
items.workedSolution: Horizontal force F_x = 24 cos(60°) = 12 N, so a_x = F_x / m = 1.2 m s⁻². Using s = ut + ½a_x t² = (1.5)(4) + 0.5(1.2)(4)² = 15.6 m.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves F cos 60° to get a_x = 1.2 m s⁻² and obtains s = 15.6 m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Resolves the towing force using F sin θ instead of the horizontal component F cos θ.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes the full cable tension F/m without resolving along the horizontal direction of motion.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the initial-velocity displacement term ut.

parts.prompt: Deduce the Boolean expression for Q in terms of the inputs and simplify it using Boolean algebra or De Morgan's laws.
parts.expectedAnswer: $Q = ((A \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})) \cdot C = A \cdot C$ (simplifies to A AND C independent of input B).
workingSteps: Write intermediate expressions at nodes D and E from the gates in the schematic.
Combine into final output $Q = ((A \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})) \cdot C = A \cdot C$.
Simplify to confirm: simplifies to A AND C independent of input B.

parts.prompt: State how many rows of the complete 8-row truth table yield output $Q = 1$.
workingSteps: Evaluate $Q = ((A \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})) \cdot C = A \cdot C$ over all 8 binary combinations.

parts.prompt: Identify the single equivalent two-input logic gate that reproduces this circuit.
parts.expectedAnswer: Single two-input AND gate on inputs A and C.
workingSteps: Match the simplified expression directly to a single two-input AND gate on inputs A and C.

items.stem: A cylindrical nichrome heating wire has diameter 0.250 mm, length 3.00 m, and resistivity 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. If the entire wire is melted down with no loss of metal and recast into a solid cube, what is the edge length of the cube?
items.workedSolution: Wire area A = πd²/4 = 4.909 × 10⁻⁸ m², so volume V = AL = 1.473 × 10⁻⁷ m³. For a solid cube of equal volume, edge s = ∛V = 5.281 × 10⁻³ m = 5.28 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 5.28 mm.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in V = πr²L.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Took the square root rather than the cube root of the volume.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π from the cylindrical wire volume.

items.stem: A pneumatic forging tup of mass 0.4 kg strikes a hardened anvil face at +12 m s⁻¹ and rebounds upward at speed 9 m s⁻¹ (opposite sign) following a 20 ms impact.

markScheme.criterion: Accounts for opposite signs of u and v in Δp = m(v − u).
Obtains J = -8.40 N s.
Divides |J| by contact time in seconds (0.02 s).
Obtains F_avg = 420 N.
Uses ½m(v² − u²).
Obtains ΔE_k = -12.6 J.

parts.prompt: Taking the incoming direction as positive, calculate the signed impulse J delivered to the object.
Calculate the magnitude of the average contact force during the impact.
Determine the signed change in kinetic energy ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i.

items.stem: A high-resistance digital voltmeter connected across an open-circuit three-cell lab supply reads 4.50 V. When a 6.00 Ω resistor is connected across the terminals, the voltmeter reading drops to 3.60 V. If the 6.00 Ω resistor is replaced by a 3.00 Ω resistor, what is the new terminal potential difference?
items.workedSolution: Open-circuit reading gives ε = 4.50 V. With R₁ = 6 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 0.6000 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.500 Ω. With R₂ = 3 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 3.000 V ≈ 3.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 1.50 Ω and computes V₂ = 3.00 V.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumed terminal potential difference stays unchanged when load resistance changes.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: During a bench test, a soldering iron cartridge runs from a regulated 18.0 V DC source at a steady current of 2.60 A for 2 min.
items.workedSolution: (a) One coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second. (b) Q = It = 312.0 C, so N = Q/e = 1.950 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.95 × 10²¹ electrons. (c) W = QV = 5.616 × 10³ J ≈ 5.62 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: States that one coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
Converts time to 120 s, computes Q = It = 312.0 C, and divides by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Correct electron count 1.95 × 10²¹.
Correct electrical work W = QV = 5.62 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Define the coulomb.
parts.expectedAnswer: The coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
workingSteps: Recall the SI definition linking electric charge, steady current, and time.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of conduction electrons passing through the device during the test.
workingSteps: Convert t = 2 × 60 = 120 s and I = 2.600 A.
Number of electrons N = Q / e = 312.0 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 1.950 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.95 × 10²¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total electrical work done by the supply during the test.

items.stem: An engine-valve spring fixture logs an initial collar reading x₁ = 28 mm ± 0.5 mm and a compressed reading x₂ = 128 mm ± 0.5 mm under force F = 18 N ± 0.8 N.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts readings to get e = 0.1 m and uses k = F / e.
Obtains k = 180 N m⁻¹.
Sums absolute uncertainties Δe = 1 mm and adds %ΔF + %Δe.
Obtains 5.44%.
Obtains Δk = 9.80 N m⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the spring constant k in N m⁻¹.
Determine the percentage uncertainty in k.
Hence find the absolute uncertainty Δk in N m⁻¹.

items.stem: An automated agricultural cable gantry drawing 2560 W hauls an implement at constant speed 4 m s⁻¹ for 50 s using a tether tension of 600 N inclined at 36.87° to the furrow.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves component F cos 36.87° and multiplies by v and t.
Obtains 9.60 × 10⁴ J.
Divides useful output power (or energy) by electrical input.
Obtains 75.0%.
Obtains E_wasted = 3.20 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the useful mechanical work done by the cable over the interval.
Calculate the percentage efficiency of the winch system.
Determine the energy wasted to the surroundings during the interval.

items.stem: A rectangular pressed graphite strip of resistivity 3.20 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m measures 45 mm long, 1.5 mm wide, and 0.6 mm thick. Calculate its resistance between the two opposite 1.5 mm × 0.6 mm end faces.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area perpendicular to current is A = w × h = (1.5 × 10⁻³ m) × (0.6 × 10⁻³ m) = 9.000 × 10⁻⁷ m², and L = 45 × 10⁻³ m. Using R = ρL/A yields 1.60 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = w × h in m² and R = ρL/A to obtain 1.60 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used the wrong cross-sectional face for the current direction.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Failed to square the mm-to-m conversion factor for area.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverted A and L in the resistance equation.

items.stem: A halogen work lamp is labelled "12 V, 24 W". What is its working electrical resistance when operating at its rated potential difference?
items.workedSolution: Using P = V² / R gives R = V² / P = 12² / 24 = 6.000 Ω ≈ 6.00 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies electrical power rating equations to obtain 6.00 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverted R = V² / P as P / V².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Used V / P instead of V² / P.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the rated current I = P / V rather than the resistance.

items.stem: In a materials testing machine, a metallic wire of length 2 m and cross-section 0.75 mm² undergoes elastic extension 1.2 mm under 126 N tension (uncertainties ±2.5% in stress and ±3% in strain).

markScheme.criterion: Converts area to m² (× 10⁻⁶) and extension to m (× 10⁻³).
Applies E = FL / (A ΔL) = σ / ε.
Obtains E = 2.80 × 10¹¹ Pa.
Sums percentage uncertainties to obtain 5.50%.
Obtains ΔE = 1.54 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

parts.prompt: Calculate the Young modulus E of the wire in pascals.
State the combined percentage uncertainty in E.
Calculate the absolute uncertainty ΔE in pascals.

items.stem: How is the electrical resistance of any two-terminal circuit component universally defined?
items.workedSolution: For both ohmic and non-ohmic components, resistance is the ratio of potential difference across a component to the current flowing through it. Verified key statement: ratio of potential difference across a component to the current flowing through it.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that ratio of potential difference across a component to the current flowing through it.

options.label: A
options.text: It is the gradient of the tangent drawn to its current against potential difference graph
options.distractorRationale: Tangent gradient gives incremental conductance dI/dV, not static resistance V/I.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the product of potential difference across the component and current through it
options.distractorRationale: The product VI defines electrical power rather than resistance.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the ratio of potential difference across a component to the current flowing through it

options.label: D
options.text: It is the reciprocal of the area enclosed under its current against voltage characteristic
options.distractorRationale: Area under an I–V curve has no physical correspondence to resistance.

items.stem: A cylindrical copper-nickel conductor conductor of diameter 1.00 mm forms part of a thermocouple extension cable and carries a steady conventional current of 2.80 A from left to right. The free-electron number density of the copper-nickel conductor is 8.10 × 10²⁸ m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 7.854 × 10⁻⁷ m² ≈ 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². (b) v = 2.75 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. (c) Because electrons are negatively charged, they drift opposite to conventional current (right to left).

markScheme.criterion: Converts diameter from mm to m and substitutes into A = πd²/4 (or πr²).
Correct cross-sectional area 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m² (4 s.f. 7.854 × 10⁻⁷ m²).
Rearranges I = nAve to v = I / (nAe) and substitutes values.
Correct final value 2.75 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.
States electrons drift opposite to conventional current (from right to left).

parts.prompt: Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire in m².
Determine the mean drift velocity of the free electrons in m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: Use v = I / (nAe) with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.prompt: State the direction of the mean drift velocity of the conduction electrons relative to the conventional current.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrons drift from right to left, opposite to conventional current.
workingSteps: Conduction electrons carry negative charge, so they move opposite to conventional current.

items.stem: A high-speed maglev test pod moving at 90 km h⁻¹ engages eddy-current brakes that provide a constant retardation of 2.5 m s⁻² for 3 s along a straight guideway. What distance in metres does the vehicle cover during this 3 s braking interval?
items.workedSolution: Convert initial speed: u = 90 / 3.6 = 25 m s⁻¹. With a = −2.5 m s⁻², s = ut + ½at² = (25)(3) − 0.5(2.5)(3)² = 63.8 m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts 90 km h⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ and evaluates s = ut − ½|a|t² = 63.8 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Mixes km h⁻¹ and m s⁻¹ by substituting the speed in km h⁻¹ directly into s = ut + ½at² without dividing by 3.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Converts speed to m s⁻¹ correctly but uses +½at² instead of −½|a|t² during braking deceleration.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in the ½at² term.

items.stem: On an electric kiln element bench, instruments record element resistance R = 10 Ω ± 0.2 Ω and terminal voltage V = 8 V ± 0.3 V.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P = V² / R.
Obtains P = 6.40 W.
Uses 2(ΔV/V) + (ΔR/R) × 100%.
Obtains 9.50%.
Obtains ΔP = 0.608 W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the nominal electrical power P dissipated in the resistor.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in P.
Determine the absolute uncertainty ΔP in watts.

items.stem: In a mechanical workshop, a structural anchor bearing sleeve is turned from solid aircraft aluminium of density 2700 kg m⁻³. It has outer diameter 48 mm, concentric central bore diameter 20 mm, and axial thickness 14 mm.
items.workedSolution: (a) V = π(R² − r²)h = 20.94 cm³ ≈ 20.9 cm³. (b) m = ρ V = 0.05653 kg ≈ 0.0565 kg. (c) density remains constant and no mass is lost when remelting or redrawing the metal.

markScheme.criterion: Uses V = π(R² − r²)h with radii and consistent unit conversion.
V = 20.9 cm³.
Applies m = ρ V in SI units.
States uniform/constant density and no mass loss.

parts.prompt: Calculate the metal volume of the annular component in cm³.
workingSteps: R = 2.4 cm, r = 1 cm, h = 1.4 cm.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of the component in kg.
State one physical assumption made when using this formula to determine the mass.
parts.expectedAnswer: It is assumed that density remains constant and no mass is lost when remelting or redrawing the metal.
workingSteps: Note uniform constant density throughout the metal with no internal voids or lost material.

items.stem: Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². A tower-crane hoist motor draws 7664 W from a three-phase supply while lifting a 300 kg steel beam vertically at steady speed through 20 m in 12 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_p = mgh with g = 9.81 m s⁻².
Obtains 5.89 × 10⁴ J.
Divides ΔE_p by P_in t and multiplies by 100%.
Obtains 64.0%.
Obtains E_wasted = 3.31 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained by the load.
Calculate the percentage efficiency of the hoisting system.
Determine the energy wasted during the lift.

items.stem: To cast a foundry crucible sample of crown gold-silver alloy with total mass 4.4 kg, a metallurgist melts together 60% gold (density 19300 kg m⁻³) and 40% silver (density 10500 kg m⁻³) by mass. Assume that the total volume of the alloy equals the sum of the constituent volumes. What is the overall density of the finished alloy in g cm⁻³?
items.workedSolution: Masses: m₁ = 2.640 kg, m₂ = 1.760 kg. Volumes: V₁ = m₁/ρ₁ = 1.368 × 10⁻⁴ m³, V₂ = m₂/ρ₂ = 1.676 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Total volume V = V₁ + V₂ = 3.044 × 10⁻⁴ m³ (304.4 cm³). Alloy density ρ = m / V = 4.4 / 3.044 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.445 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.45 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ (14.5 g cm⁻³).

markScheme.criterion: Correct harmonic-mean alloy density = 14.5 g cm⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses an incorrect geometric factor or lever-arm ratio.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the volume-weighted arithmetic average instead of harmonic mean for a mass-fraction mix.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the mass percentages assigned to the two constituent metals.

items.stem: In a process-engineering calibration, 2 kg of glycerol (c = 2400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) warms by 30 K when heated for 80 s by a 2118 W resistive element.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into Q = mcΔT.
Obtains Q = 1.44 × 10⁵ J.
Subtracts Q from total electrical energy P_in t.
Obtains E_lost = 2.54 × 10⁴ J.
Obtains η = 85.0%.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy Q absorbed by the sample.
Calculate the thermal energy lost to the surroundings during the heating interval.
Determine the percentage efficiency of the heating arrangement.

items.stem: A solid solid copper ballast block (density 8930 kg m⁻³) of mass 22.5 kg is suspended from a calibrated spring balance and lowered until it is completely submerged in freshwater of density 1000 kg m⁻³ without touching the tank floor (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) the upward buoyancy force equals the weight of fluid displaced by the body. (b) V = 2.520 × 10⁻³ m³ ⇒ F_B = 24.72 N ≈ 24.7 N. (c) W_app = W − F_B = 196.0 N ≈ 196 N.

markScheme.criterion: Upthrust equals weight of displaced fluid.
Finds V = m / ρ_obj and applies F_B = ρ_fluid V g.
Subtracts upthrust from weight in air.
Apparent weight = 196 N.

parts.prompt: State Archimedes' principle.
parts.expectedAnswer: Archimedes' principle states that the upward buoyancy force equals the weight of fluid displaced by the body.
workingSteps: State that upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced by the immersed body.

parts.prompt: Calculate the upthrust acting on the completely submerged block.
Hence calculate the reading on the spring balance while the block remains fully submerged.
workingSteps: Spring balance tension = W − F_B = 196.0 N ≈ 196 N.

items.stem: Two students calibrate a digital balance using a certified reference mass. Student A obtains readings shown in the target diagram, tightly clustered but all shifted above the true value.
items.workedSolution: (a) Precision describes small spread between repeated measurements; accuracy describes closeness to the true value; the dataset shows high precision with systematic error and low accuracy. (b) Repeating and averaging only reduces random scatter; to fix systematic offset, identify and subtract zero error or recalibrate the instrument.

markScheme.criterion: Precision: closeness of repeated readings to each other / mean (small random spread).
Accuracy: closeness of measurement to the true value.
Identify high precision with systematic error and low accuracy.
Explain that systematic error shifts every reading identically so repeats/mean do not remove it.
State remedy: tare/zero, identify and subtract zero error or recalibrate the instrument.

parts.expectedAnswer: Precision is closeness of repeated readings to each other / their mean; accuracy is closeness of a measured value to the true value. Student A's readings exhibit high precision with systematic error and low accuracy.

Define accuracy in terms of closeness to the true value.
Classify the plotted cluster as high precision with systematic error and low accuracy.

parts.expectedAnswer: A systematic error shifts every reading by the same fixed offset so averaging preserves that offset; Student A must identify and subtract zero error or recalibrate the instrument.
