Specify zeroing/taring or subtracting the zero error to restore accuracy.

items.stem: A vertical titanium rod experiences a uniform stretching load in a materials laboratory.
items.workedSolution: (a) tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area. (b) area must be specified explicitly as cross sectional area perpendicular to the applied force. Core principle: cross sectional area distinguishes tensile stress from surface area pressure.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to cross sectional area distinguishes tensile stress from surface area pressure.
States primary causal step: area must be specified explicitly as cross sectional area perpendicular to the applied force.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (area must be specified explicitly as cross sectional area perpendicular to the applied force).

parts.prompt: Define tensile stress with complete NCUK mark-scheme precision. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area.
workingSteps: Establish the core NCUK mark point: tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area.
Anchor concept: cross sectional area distinguishes tensile stress from surface area pressure.

parts.prompt: Explain why specifying cross-sectional area is essential and state the SI unit of tensile stress. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: area must be specified explicitly as cross sectional area perpendicular to the applied force.
workingSteps: Develop the causal explanation clearly without algebraic shortcuts: area must be specified explicitly as cross sectional area perpendicular to the applied force.
Avoid the common error of writing force per unit area without specifying cross sectional area.

items.stem: Under what essential physical condition is the current through a metallic conductor directly proportional to the potential difference across it?
items.workedSolution: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant. Verified key statement: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.

options.label: A
options.text: Specifically, Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant

options.label: B
options.text: Specifically, Ohm law applies to every circuit component regardless of temperature or heating
options.distractorRationale: Non-ohmic components and heated filaments violate direct proportionality.

options.label: C
options.text: Specifically, Ohm law applies only when current flows through a vacuum rather than a solid metal
options.distractorRationale: Metallic conductors at constant temperature are the primary ohmic devices.

options.label: D
options.text: Specifically, Ohm law applies only when a variable resistor increases circuit temperature smoothly
options.distractorRationale: Changing temperature changes metal resistivity and breaks linearity.

items.stem: A student converts the ohm into alternative SI derived and base unit expressions.
items.workedSolution: (a) volt per ampere and joule second per coulomb squared. (b) base unit form combines kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere squared. Core principle: resistance is potential difference divided by current.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: volt per ampere and joule second per coulomb squared.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to resistance is potential difference divided by current.
States primary causal step: base unit form combines kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere squared.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (substituting joule per coulomb for volt and coulomb per second for ampere gives joule second per coulomb squared).

parts.prompt: State two derived unit forms equivalent to the ohm from resistance and potential difference definitions. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: volt per ampere and joule second per coulomb squared.

items.stem: Two ideal cells are connected in series with their positive terminals facing each other inside a single closed loop with two resistors. How does Kirchhoff's second law treat their electromotive forces?
items.workedSolution: In Kirchhoff's loop rule, opposing cells subtract algebraically when traversing the loop in a consistent direction. Verified key statement: opposing cells subtract algebraically when traversing the loop in a consistent direction.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that opposing cells subtract algebraically when traversing the loop in a consistent direction.

options.text: When summing around the loop, opposing cells always add together to double the net circuit electromotive force
options.distractorRationale: Opposing polarities push charge in opposite directions around the loop, so their emfs subtract.

options.label: B
options.text: When summing around the loop, opposing cells subtract algebraically when traversing the loop in a consistent direction

options.label: C
options.text: When summing around the loop, the smaller cell is ignored completely while the larger cell drives the entire current
options.distractorRationale: Both cells contribute algebraically to the net emf around the loop.

options.label: D
options.text: When summing around the loop, current cannot flow unless both cells have identical electromotive force
options.distractorRationale: If the emfs differ, the difference drives current around the loop; equal opposing cells give zero net emf.

items.stem: A micrometer screw gauge has a constant positive zero error that the experimenter forgets to subtract. Repeating the wire diameter measurement many times produces closely clustered readings. What is the effect of averaging?
items.workedSolution: Averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error. Verified key statement: averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error.

options.label: A
options.text: In this situation, averaging repeated measurements eliminates the zero error and makes the mean completely accurate
options.distractorRationale: Every reading shares the same positive offset, so the mean still carries the exact zero error.

options.label: B
options.text: In this situation, repeating measurements worsens random scatter without improving precision
options.distractorRationale: Repeating and averaging reduces random scatter and improves precision.

options.label: C
options.text: In this situation, averaging repeated measurements improves precision against random scatter but cannot remove a systematic zero error

options.label: D

items.workedSolution: (a) time constant equals resistance multiplied by capacitance so lowering resistance reduces the time constant. (b) charge leaves the plates more rapidly so after any given elapsed interval the remaining potential difference is lower. Core principle: shorter time constant produces a steeper exponential decay curve.

items.stem: A steel ball bearing is released from rest at the surface of a tall column of viscous glycerol. Why does it eventually move downward at a constant terminal velocity?
items.workedSolution: Initially weight exceeds drag, then drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero. Verified key statement: drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero.

options.label: A
options.text: As the sphere accelerates, gravitational pull weakens with depth until the weight vanishes completely
options.distractorRationale: Weight stays constant near Earth's surface; acceleration stops because forces balance, not because gravity vanishes.

options.label: B
options.text: As the sphere accelerates, upward viscous drag stays constant while kinetic energy reaches a fluid ceiling
options.distractorRationale: Viscous drag is speed-dependent and grows until it balances weight (and upthrust).

options.label: C
options.text: As the sphere accelerates, drag increases with speed until upward drag equals downward weight making resultant force and acceleration zero

options.label: D
options.text: As the sphere accelerates, upward drag exceeds weight so the ball moves steadily without net force
options.distractorRationale: If drag exceeded weight, the resultant force would point upward and decelerate the sphere.

items.stem: A racing car travels around a flat circular track at constant speed.
items.workedSolution: (a) velocity is a vector so constant speed along a circular path still involves continuous velocity change and acceleration. (b) because force is always perpendicular to instantaneous displacement the centripetal force does zero work and kinetic energy remains constant. Core principle: centripetal force alters direction of velocity without changing speed.

Includes exact NCUK precision linked to centripetal force alters direction of velocity without changing speed.

Completes full physical linkage without misconception (resultant centripetal force and acceleration always point perpendicular to instantaneous velocity toward the centre of the circle).

items.stem: By dimensional homogeneity, the transverse wave speed v along a taut cable depends only on tension T (in N, i.e. kg m s⁻²) and linear mass density μ (mass per unit length) via v = Tᵃ μᵇ with dimensionless constant equal to unity. In an acoustic wire rig, T = 216 N ± 1.5 N and μ = 12 g m⁻¹ ± 0.15 g m⁻¹. What is the percentage uncertainty in the wave speed v deduced from dimensional homogeneity?
items.workedSolution: Dimensional homogeneity gives v = T^(1/2) μ^(−1/2). Hence %Δv = ½(%ΔT) + ½(%Δμ) = 0.5(1.5/216 + 0.15/12) × 100% = 0.972%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses exponents |1/2| and |−1/2| to obtain %Δv = 0.972%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Sums %ΔT + %Δμ without multiplying by the 1/2 power factor from the square-root exponents.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainties because μ appears in the denominator of √(T/μ).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the combined percentage uncertainty by 2 instead of 1/2 for a square-root power.

items.stem: A biochemistry ultracentrifuge calibration head travels at tangential speed 6 m s⁻¹ ± 0.5 m s⁻¹ on a rotor path of radius 1.2 m ± 0.05 m, experiencing radial acceleration a = v² / r. What is the absolute uncertainty Δa in the centripetal acceleration?
items.workedSolution: Nominal acceleration a = v²/r = 6² / 1.2 = 30.0 m s⁻². Fractional uncertainty Δa/a = 2(0.5/6) + (0.05/1.2) = 0.208. Absolute uncertainty Δa = a(Δa/a) = 6.25 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Calculates a = v²/r and multiplies by 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) to obtain Δa = 6.25 m s⁻².

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to double Δv/v for the squared v² factor before multiplying by a.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes absolute uncertainties (Δv)² / Δr directly into the formula v² / r.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Stops at the dimensionless fractional uncertainty Δa/a without multiplying by a = v²/r.

items.stem: During a Required Practical wire check, micrometer readings give wire diameter d = 0.6 mm ± 0.02 mm under suspended tension F = 90 N ± 2 N. What is the percentage uncertainty in the tensile stress σ = 4F / (πd²)?
items.workedSolution: In σ = 4F / (πd²), the constant 4/π has zero uncertainty, so %Δσ = %ΔF + 2(%Δd) = (2/90 + 2 × 0.02/0.6) × 100% = 8.89%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates %ΔF + 2(%Δd) = 8.89%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the power exponent 2 on d² when propagating uncertainty in A = πd²/4.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts 2(%Δd) from %ΔF because d² sits in the denominator of 4F/(πd²).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies %Δd by the constant prefactor 4 in 4F/(πd²) instead of by the exponent 2.

items.stem: Consider a deep-sea research submersible observation hatch, which has a flat horizontal surface of area 2.2 m² situated at a depth of 31.5 m beneath the open surface of seawater of density 1025 kg m⁻³. Take atmospheric pressure at the free surface as 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the total absolute pressure acting on the submerged surface in kPa?
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1025 × 9.81 × 31.5 = 3.167 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 3.17 × 10⁵ Pa. Absolute pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 3.167 × 10⁵ = 4.177 × 10⁵ Pa = 417.7 kPa ≈ 418 kPa. Total force F = p_abs A = 4.177 × 10⁵ × 2.2 = 9.190 × 10⁵ N ≈ 9.19 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 418 kPa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only gauge pressure ρgh and omits atmospheric pressure.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to multiply by g = 9.81 m s⁻².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts atmospheric pressure instead of adding it.

items.stem: How is the centre of gravity of a rigid object defined?
items.workedSolution: The centre of gravity is the point through which the entire weight of a body appears to act. Verified key statement: point through which the entire weight of a body appears to act.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that point through which the entire weight of a body appears to act.

options.distractorRationale: Fails for non-uniform or asymmetric objects whose mass distribution is uneven.

options.label: B

options.distractorRationale: Confuses support contact point with the effective point of application of weight.

options.label: C
options.text: The point inside the material where gravitational field strength reaches a maximum
options.distractorRationale: Near Earth the gravitational field is uniform; centre of gravity can even lie outside hollow shapes like a ring.

items.stem: During quality inspection of a syntactic-foam subsea buoyancy block, a technician measures the cubic specimen to have edge length 8 cm ± 0.08 cm and mass 2760 g ± 2 g. What is the absolute uncertainty Δρ in the density when expressed in kg m⁻³?

items.stem: During an aerospace radome hail-impact simulation, an ice sphere of mass 1.5 kg hits a flat target perpendicularly at +15 m s⁻¹ and rebounds directly opposite at 12 m s⁻¹ (v = −12 m s⁻¹) with contact time 5 ms. What is the magnitude of the average force exerted on the object during the 5 ms impact?
items.workedSolution: Taking incoming velocity as +15 m s⁻¹ and rebound velocity as −12 m s⁻¹, |Δp| = 1.5(15 + 12) = 40.5 N s. With Δt = 5 × 10⁻³ = 0.005 s, F_avg = |Δp| / Δt = 8.10 × 10³ N.

items.stem: An ideal voltmeter placed directly across the terminals of a robotics test battery on open circuit reads 8.00 V. When a 7.00 Ω load resistor is connected across the battery, the voltmeter reading falls to 7.00 V. The first load is then removed and replaced by a 3.00 Ω load resistor.
items.workedSolution: (a) I₁ = 1.000 A, so r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 1.000 Ω ≈ 1.00 Ω. (b) I₂ = 2.000 A, giving V₂ = I₂R₂ = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 1.00 A and substitutes into r = (ε − V₁) / I₁.
Correct internal resistance 1.00 Ω.
Uses V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) (or finds I₂ then I₂R₂).
Correct terminal potential difference 6.00 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.
workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 7 / 7 = 1.000 A.
Internal resistance r = (ε − V₁) / I₁ = (8 − 7) / 1.000 A = 1.000 Ω ≈ 1.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new terminal potential difference across the 3.00 Ω resistor.
workingSteps: New current I₂ = ε / (R₂ + r) = 8 / (3 + 1.000 Ω) = 2.000 A.
Terminal pd V₂ = I₂ R₂ = 2.000 A × 3 = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V.

items.stem: A portable LED lantern connected across a 6.00 V supply draws a constant current of 240 mA for 4.5 min. How many electrons pass a fixed cross-section of the connecting wire in this time?
items.workedSolution: Convert time t = 4.5 × 60 = 270 s and current I = 0.2400 A. Total charge Q = It = 64.80 C. Number of electrons N = Q / e = 64.80 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 4.050 × 10²⁰ ≈ 4.05 × 10²⁰.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 4.05 × 10²⁰.

items.stem: During calibration of a railway buffer spring scale, a technician records datum position x₁ = 14 mm ± 0.8 mm before loading and x₂ = 74 mm ± 0.8 mm when axial force F = 36 N ± 0.5 N is applied. What is the absolute uncertainty Δk in the spring constant expressed in N m⁻¹?
items.workedSolution: Extension e = (74 − 14) × 10⁻³ = 0.06 m with Δe = 2(0.8) × 10⁻³ = 0.0016 m. Nominal k = 36 / 0.06 = 600 N m⁻¹. Fractional uncertainty Δk/k = 0.5/36 + 0.0016/0.06 = 0.0406, so Δk = 24.3 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines Δe = 2Δx with ΔF/F + Δe/e to obtain Δk = 24.3 N m⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the operating resistance of the component.
Calculate the electrical energy transferred in 5 min.

items.stem: In a Searle's-apparatus wire practical below the limit of proportionality, a wire of original length 2 m and cross-sectional area 0.75 mm² extends by 1.2 mm under tensile load 90 N; tensile stress has uncertainty ±2.5% and tensile strain has uncertainty ±3%. What is the Young modulus E of the wire in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Tensile stress σ = F / A = 90 / (0.75 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.20 × 10⁸ Pa. Tensile strain ε = ΔL / L = (1.2 × 10⁻³) / 2 = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴. Young modulus E = σ / ε = 2.00 × 10¹¹ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates σ = F/A and ε = ΔL/L in SI units to obtain E = 2.00 × 10¹¹ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Converts mm² to m² using 10⁻³ instead of (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁶, underestimating stress and Young modulus by 10³.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets both mm² → 10⁻⁶ m² and mm → 10⁻³ m unit prefix powers properly.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies tensile stress by tensile strain (σ × ε) instead of dividing σ / ε.

items.stem: Electrical components impede charge flow to varying degrees characterized in ohms.
items.workedSolution: (a) The ohm is the resistance of a conductor carrying a current of one ampere under a potential difference of one volt. Full mark-scheme anchors: ratio of potential difference to current equal to one volt per ampere; steady current of one ampere flows when potential difference across the conductor is one volt.

markScheme.criterion: States key physical element: ratio of potential difference to current equal to one volt per ampere.
Completes canonical precision: steady current of one ampere flows when potential difference across the conductor is one volt.

parts.prompt: Define the ohm. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: The ohm is the resistance of a conductor carrying a current of one ampere under a potential difference of one volt.
workingSteps: Recall the exact NCUK rubric anchor: ohm is one volt per ampere.

Include both essential marking elements: ratio of potential difference to current equal to one volt per ampere and steady current of one ampere flows when potential difference across the conductor is one volt.

items.stem: In a bench power busbar, a uniform cylindrical annealed copper wire of diameter 0.600 mm carries a steady current of 1.80 A. The free-electron number density in the annealed copper is 8.50 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the mean drift speed of the conduction electrons.
items.workedSolution: Convert diameter to metres: d = 6.000 × 10⁻⁴ m. Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = 2.827 × 10⁻⁷ m². Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives v = I / (nAe) = 4.681 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 4.68 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 4.68 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in A = πr² (four times too large an area).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied by 4 instead of dividing by 4 in A = πd²/4.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π when calculating the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: An intercity electric express train cruising along a straight level track at 54 km h⁻¹ applies regenerative brakes producing a uniform deceleration of 2.5 m s⁻² for 5 s.

markScheme.criterion: Divides 54 by 3.6 to obtain u = 15 m s⁻¹ and applies v = u − |a|t.
Obtains v = 2.50 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½|a|t² or ½(u + v)t with SI units.
Obtains s = 43.8 m.
Obtains v_mean = 8.75 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Convert the initial speed into m s⁻¹ and calculate the speed at the end of the braking interval.
Calculate the distance travelled during the braking interval.
Determine the mean speed over this interval in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A laboratory manganin standard resistor of resistance R = 6 Ω ± 0.4 Ω carries a steady potential difference of V = 48 V ± 0.2 V. What is the nominal electrical power dissipated in the resistor?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates P = V²/R = 384 W.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes current I = V / R instead of electrical power P = V² / R.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies V × R (confusing V = IR with P = VI).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes V²R (confusing I²R with V²/R).

items.stem: In a mechanical workshop, a heavy flanged thrust washer is turned from solid stainless steel of density 7870 kg m⁻³. It has outer diameter 44 mm, concentric central bore diameter 30 mm, and axial thickness 22 mm. What is the mass of this annular component in grams?
items.workedSolution: Outer radius R = 22 mm = 0.02200 m; inner radius r = 15 mm = 0.01500 m; thickness h = 0.02200 m. Volume V = π(R² − r²)h = 1.790 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (17.90 cm³). Mass m = ρ V = 0.1409 kg = 140.9 g ≈ 141 g.

markScheme.criterion: Correct mass = 141 g.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses outer and inner diameters instead of radii in π(R² − r²), inflating area by 4×.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats the washer as a solid cylinder and omits the central hole.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes π(R − r)² instead of π(R² − r²).

items.stem: Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². A tower-crane hoist motor draws 7664 W from a three-phase supply while lifting a 300 kg steel beam vertically at steady speed through 20 m in 12 s. What is the percentage efficiency of the lifting system?
items.workedSolution: Useful gravitational potential energy ΔE_p = mgh = 300 × 9.81 × 20 = 5.89 × 10⁴ J. Input electrical energy E_in = 7664 × 12 = 91968 J. Efficiency η = (ΔE_p / E_in) × 100% = 64.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgh / (P_in t) × 100% with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 64.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits gravitational field strength g when computing gravitational potential energy mgh.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input energy wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides useful energy mgh in joules directly by input power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

items.stem: To cast an antique-restoration metal sample of heavy tungsten-steel alloy with total mass 4.8 kg, a metallurgist melts together 60% tungsten (density 19250 kg m⁻³) and 40% iron (density 7870 kg m⁻³) by mass. Assume that the total volume of the alloy equals the sum of the constituent volumes.
items.workedSolution: (a) Density is mass per unit volume of a material. (b) V₁ + V₂ = 393.6 cm³ ≈ 394 cm³. (c) ρ = m / V = 1.220 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.22 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Defines density as mass per unit volume.
Finds both constituent masses and sums V₁ = m₁/ρ₁ and V₂ = m₂/ρ₂.
Total volume = 394 cm³.
Converts cm³ to m³ (× 10⁻⁶) and divides total mass by total volume.
Alloy density = 1.22 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³.

parts.prompt: Define the density of a substance.
parts.expectedAnswer: Density is defined as mass per unit volume of a material.
workingSteps: State that density is mass divided by volume.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total volume of the cast alloy sample in cm³.
Hence calculate the overall density of the alloy in kg m⁻³.

items.stem: In a process-engineering calibration, 2 kg of silicone heat-transfer oil (c = 1800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) warms by 30 K when heated for 80 s by a 1800 W resistive element. How much thermal energy is lost to the surroundings during the 80 s heating period?
items.workedSolution: Electrical energy supplied E_in = P_in t = 1800 × 80 = 144000 J. Thermal energy retained by sample Q = mcΔT = 2 × 1800 × 30 = 108000 J. Energy lost to surroundings = E_in − Q = 3.60 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mcΔT (108000 J) from P_in t (144000 J) to obtain 3.60 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the thermal energy absorbed by the sample Q = mcΔT rather than the heat lost to the surroundings.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the total electrical energy supplied P_in t instead of subtracting mcΔT.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the rate of heat loss in watts without multiplying by the heating time t.

items.stem: A solid machined titanium ballast block (density 4510 kg m⁻³) of mass 22.5 kg is suspended from a calibrated spring balance and lowered until it is completely submerged in seawater of density 1025 kg m⁻³ without touching the tank floor (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the upward buoyancy force (upthrust) acting on the submerged block?
items.workedSolution: Block volume V = m / ρ_obj = 22.5 / 4510 = 4.989 × 10⁻³ m³. Upthrust F_B = ρ_fluid V g = 1025 × 4.989 × 10⁻³ × 9.81 = 50.16 N ≈ 50.2 N. Apparent weight W_app = m g − F_B = 220.7 − 50.16 = 170.6 N ≈ 171 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value = 50.2 N.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses object density instead of fluid density, recovering the object's own weight.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reports apparent weight instead of upthrust.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes displaced mass in kg without multiplying by g = 9.81 m s⁻².

items.stem: The target diagram shows six repeated readings of a resistor value made with a digital ohmmeter that had a non-zero lead resistance. Which description best classifies this dataset?
items.workedSolution: Tightly grouped dots indicate high precision (small spread about the mean), while the constant offset from the true centre reveals a systematic zero error and low accuracy. Therefore option A is correct: high precision with systematic error and low accuracy.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: high precision with systematic error and low accuracy.

options.label: A
options.text: The readings show high precision with systematic error and low accuracy

options.label: B
options.text: The readings show low precision with random error and an accurate mean
options.distractorRationale: The points are tightly clustered together (high precision) yet consistently displaced from the true value.

options.label: C
options.text: The readings show high precision and high accuracy with negligible bias
options.distractorRationale: Tight clustering establishes precision only, not closeness to the true centre value.

options.label: D
options.text: The readings show low precision caused by random human error
options.distractorRationale: Tightly grouped readings indicate small random scatter, and 'human error' is rejected by AQA mark schemes.

items.stem: Which definition of tensile stress in a stretched metal wire meets full NCUK mark-scheme precision?
items.workedSolution: Tensile stress is the tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area. Verified key statement: tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area.

options.label: A
options.text: It is the tensile force acting per unit total outer surface area of the wire
options.distractorRationale: Uses cylindrical surface area instead of cross-sectional area perpendicular to the load.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the extension produced per unit original length of the stretched wire
options.distractorRationale: Defines tensile strain rather than tensile stress.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the tensile force acting per unit cross sectional area

options.label: D
options.text: It is the product of tensile force and cross sectional area of the wire
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies force by area instead of dividing force by cross-sectional area.

items.stem: A student measures current and potential difference for a uniform resistance wire to verify Ohm's law.
items.workedSolution: (a) Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant. (b) keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.

parts.prompt: State the physical condition required for Ohm's law to remain valid. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.
workingSteps: Identify the primary physical statement: Ohm law applies only when temperature and physical conditions remain constant.

parts.prompt: State one practical precaution to prevent heating of the wire during measurements. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.
workingSteps: Link the physical principle (limiting current prevents self heating from distorting a linear ohmic plot) to the required condition or mechanism: keeping currents small and switching off between readings minimises heating of the resistance wire.

items.stem: Which statement correctly matches the farad and the watt to their equivalent SI combinations?
items.workedSolution: From C = Q / V and P = E / t, the units are coulomb per volt for capacitance and joule per second for power. Verified key statement: coulomb per volt for capacitance and joule per second for power.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that coulomb per volt for capacitance and joule per second for power.

options.label: A
options.text: They correspond to coulomb per volt for capacitance and joule per second for power

options.label: B
options.text: They correspond to volt per coulomb for capacitance and joule second for power
options.distractorRationale: Inverts capacitance C = Q / V and multiplies energy by time instead of dividing.

options.label: C
options.text: They correspond to coulomb volt for capacitance and volt per ampere for power
options.distractorRationale: Uses product QV for capacitance and resistance units for power.

options.label: D
options.text: They correspond to ampere per volt for capacitance and coulomb per second for power
options.distractorRationale: Confuses capacitance with conductance and power with electric current.

items.stem: To measure the potential difference across a resistor accurately without disturbing a DC circuit, how should an ideal voltmeter be wired and what resistance should it have?
items.workedSolution: An ideal voltmeter is connected in parallel with infinite resistance so zero current bypasses the resistor. Verified key statement: connected in parallel with infinite resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that connected in parallel with infinite resistance.

options.label: A
options.text: It must be connected in series with infinite resistance
options.distractorRationale: Wiring an infinite-resistance meter in series would block circuit current completely.

options.label: B
options.text: It must be connected in parallel with infinite resistance

options.label: C
options.text: It must be connected in parallel with zero resistance
options.distractorRationale: A zero-resistance parallel meter would short-circuit the resistor.

options.label: D
options.text: It must be connected in series with zero resistance
options.distractorRationale: Describes the wiring and resistance of an ideal ammeter instead of a voltmeter.

items.stem: Three branches meet at a soldered node in a direct-current circuit.
items.workedSolution: (a) algebraic sum of currents meeting at any circuit junction is zero. (b) consequence of conservation of electric charge because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that algebraic sum of currents meeting at any circuit junction is zero.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that consequence of conservation of electric charge because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.

parts.prompt: State Kirchhoff's first law. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: algebraic sum of currents meeting at any circuit junction is zero.
workingSteps: Identify the primary physical statement: algebraic sum of currents meeting at any circuit junction is zero.

parts.prompt: State the fundamental conservation law that it represents. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: consequence of conservation of electric charge because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.
workingSteps: Link the physical principle (junction current rule follows directly from charge conservation) to the required condition or mechanism: consequence of conservation of electric charge because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.

items.stem: Which wording gives the canonical NCUK definition of the coulomb?
items.workedSolution: From Q = I t, the coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second. Verified key statement: charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.

options.label: A
options.text: The rate of flow of electric charge past a point each second
options.distractorRationale: Defines electric current (the ampere) rather than electric charge (the coulomb).

options.label: B
options.text: The electrical energy transferred per volt of potential difference across a wire
options.distractorRationale: Gives joules per volt, which does not express the base-unit definition of the coulomb via ampere and second.

options.label: C
options.text: The charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second

options.label: D
options.text: The force exerted between two stationary point charges placed unit distance apart
options.distractorRationale: Confuses the coulomb unit of charge with Coulomb law of electrostatic force.

items.stem: Two pucks collide on a frictionless air table in an isolated laboratory demonstration.
items.workedSolution: (a) total linear momentum is conserved in every isolated collision regardless of elasticity. (b) total kinetic energy before equals total kinetic energy after only in an elastic collision.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that total linear momentum is conserved in every isolated collision regardless of elasticity.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that total kinetic energy before equals total kinetic energy after only in an elastic collision.

parts.prompt: State what happens to total linear momentum in both elastic and inelastic impacts. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: total linear momentum is conserved in every isolated collision regardless of elasticity.
workingSteps: Identify the primary physical statement: total linear momentum is conserved in every isolated collision regardless of elasticity.

parts.prompt: State the kinetic energy criterion that distinguishes an elastic impact from an inelastic one. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: total kinetic energy before equals total kinetic energy after only in an elastic collision.
workingSteps: Link the physical principle (comparing total kinetic energy before and after tests whether a collision is elastic) to the required condition or mechanism: total kinetic energy before equals total kinetic energy after only in an elastic collision.

items.stem: A laboratory battery with internal resistance supplies a variable resistor while a high-resistance voltmeter monitors the battery terminals.
items.workedSolution: (a) decreasing external load resistance lowers total circuit resistance and increases current drawn from the cell. (b) since cell electromotive force stays constant the measured terminal potential difference falls. Core principle: terminal potential difference equals constant electromotive force minus internal lost volts.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: decreasing external load resistance lowers total circuit resistance and increases current drawn from the cell.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to terminal potential difference equals constant electromotive force minus internal lost volts.
States primary causal step: since cell electromotive force stays constant the measured terminal potential difference falls.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (greater current produces a larger potential drop or lost volts across the internal resistance).

parts.prompt: Without calculation, state and explain how reducing the external variable resistance affects the circuit current and internal lost volts. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: decreasing external load resistance lowers total circuit resistance and increases current drawn from the cell.
workingSteps: Establish the core NCUK mark point: decreasing external load resistance lowers total circuit resistance and increases current drawn from the cell.
Anchor concept: terminal potential difference equals constant electromotive force minus internal lost volts.

parts.prompt: Without calculation, explain why the terminal potential difference falls while the electromotive force stays constant. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: since cell electromotive force stays constant the measured terminal potential difference falls.
workingSteps: Develop the causal explanation clearly without algebraic shortcuts: since cell electromotive force stays constant the measured terminal potential difference falls.
Avoid the common error of assuming terminal potential difference remains constant equal to electromotive force as load current increases.

items.stem: A light-dependent resistor is connected in series with a fixed resistor across an ideal DC supply. A bright lamp is switched on above the sensor. Without calculation, what is the immediate response?
items.workedSolution: For an illuminated LDR, brighter light releases more charge carriers reducing light dependent resistor resistance so circuit current rises and its voltage share decreases. Verified key statement: brighter light releases more charge carriers reducing light dependent resistor resistance so circuit current rises and its voltage share decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that brighter light releases more charge carriers reducing light dependent resistor resistance so circuit current rises and its voltage share decreases.

options.label: A
options.text: Under illumination, incident photons block electron motion increasing light dependent resistor resistance and lowering current
options.distractorRationale: Light frees additional charge carriers in an LDR, lowering rather than raising its resistance.

options.label: B
options.text: Under illumination, resistance falls so potential difference across the light dependent resistor increases
options.distractorRationale: A smaller resistance receives a smaller fraction of the fixed supply voltage.

options.label: C
options.text: Under illumination, circuit current stays constant because the fixed resistor governs the whole loop
options.distractorRationale: Total series resistance equals the sum of both resistances, so reducing LDR resistance raises total current.

options.label: D
options.text: Under illumination, brighter light releases more charge carriers reducing light dependent resistor resistance so circuit current rises and its voltage share decreases

items.stem: A technician compares two CRO adjustments when characterising a sinusoidal laboratory generator output. Which statement accurately describes the effect of the time-base control?
items.workedSolution: Correct experimental practice: Reduce the time base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty and switching time base off produces a vertical line of height peak to peak voltage.

markScheme.criterion: Reduce the time base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty and switching time base off produces a vertical line of height peak to peak voltage.

options.label: A
options.text: Switching time-base off produces a vertical line of height equal to peak voltage V₀ rather than peak-to-peak voltage.
options.distractorRationale: The beam swings from −V₀ to +V₀, giving total vertical length 2V₀ = V_pp.

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing the time-base setting decreases the actual frequency of the alternating generator.
options.distractorRationale: Adjusting CRO time-base changes only the display horizontal scale, never the source frequency.

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce the time base setting to stretch the waveform horizontally for lower percentage uncertainty and switching time base off produces a vertical line of height peak to peak voltage.

options.label: D
options.text: Switching time-base off converts the alternating supply into a constant direct current voltage.
options.distractorRationale: The supply remains alternating; only the horizontal sweep voltage inside the CRO stops.

items.stem: Why should a student turn the ratchet rather than the main thimble when closing a micrometer screw gauge onto a soft copper wire, and why must diameter be measured at multiple orientations?
items.workedSolution: Correct experimental practice: Use the ratchet to avoid over tightening or compressing the wire and repeat orthogonal diameter measurements along the length to detect non-circularity.

markScheme.criterion: Use the ratchet to avoid over tightening or compressing the wire and repeat orthogonal diameter measurements along the length to detect non-circularity.

items.stem: Vernier callipers of resolution 0.05 mm measure the external diameter of a brass pendulum bob. The vernier zero lies just past 18 mm and vernier division 7 aligns directly with a main-scale mark. The closed-jaw zero error is +0.05 mm. What is the corrected dimension?
items.workedSolution: Raw Vernier reading $= 18 + 7 \times 0.05 = 18.35$ mm. Correcting for zero error (+0.05 mm): $18.35 - (+0.05) = 18.30$ mm.

markScheme.criterion: Corrected Vernier reading $= 18.30$ mm (18.30 mm).

items.stem: Capacitors store separated electric charge on conducting plates across a dielectric.
items.workedSolution: (a) The farad is the capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates. Full mark-scheme anchors: charge stored on one plate per unit potential difference across the capacitor; one coulomb of charge stored when potential difference across the plates is one volt.

markScheme.criterion: States key physical element: charge stored on one plate per unit potential difference across the capacitor.
Completes canonical precision: one coulomb of charge stored when potential difference across the plates is one volt.

parts.prompt: Define the farad. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: The farad is the capacitance storing one coulomb of charge per volt of potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: Recall the exact NCUK rubric anchor: capacitance equals charge stored divided by potential difference.

Include both essential marking elements: charge stored on one plate per unit potential difference across the capacitor and one coulomb of charge stored when potential difference across the plates is one volt.

items.stem: In a chemical-process storage column (g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹ exact), a diaphragm gauge sits at depth h = 60 m ± 0.3 m below the free surface of a liquid of density ρ = 900 kg m⁻³ ± 25 kg m⁻³. What is the hydrostatic gauge pressure p = ρgh at this depth in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure p = ρgh = 900 × 9.81 × 60 = 5.30 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates p = ρgh = 5.30 × 10⁵ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes ρh and omits gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reports the numerical value in kilopascals while labelling the unit as pascals.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides ρg by depth h instead of multiplying ρgh.

items.stem: By dimensional homogeneity, the transverse wave speed v along a taut cable depends only on tension T (in N, i.e. kg m s⁻²) and linear mass density μ (mass per unit length) via v = Tᵃ μᵇ with dimensionless constant equal to unity. In an acoustic wire rig, T = 120 N ± 2 N and μ = 4 g m⁻¹ ± 0.2 g m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Equates SI base dimensions kg, m, s to deduce a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.
Converts linear density to 0.004 kg m⁻¹ and substitutes into √(T/μ).
Obtains v = 173 m s⁻¹.
Multiplies both %ΔT and %Δμ by 1/2 before adding.
Obtains 3.33%.
Obtains Δv = 5.77 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: By equating SI base units on both sides of v = Tᵃ μᵇ, determine a and b and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
workingSteps: [T] = kg m s⁻² and [μ] = kg m⁻¹ ⇒ kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, so a = 0.5 and b = −0.5.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in v.
Determine the absolute uncertainty Δv in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A biochemistry ultracentrifuge calibration head travels at tangential speed 18 m s⁻¹ ± 0.15 m s⁻¹ on a rotor path of radius 1.5 m ± 0.08 m, experiencing radial acceleration a = v² / r.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes v and r into a = v² / r.
Obtains a = 216 m s⁻².
Uses 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) and converts to a percentage.
Obtains 7.00%.
Obtains Δa = 15.1 m s⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the nominal centripetal acceleration a.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a.
Determine the absolute uncertainty Δa.

items.stem: Using a digital micrometer, a student measures the diameter of a cylindrical constantan wire as d = 1.2 mm ± 0.01 mm while hanging a calibrated tensile load F = 45 N ± 0.8 N from it.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 with d converted from mm to m.
Obtains σ = 3.98 × 10⁷ Pa.
Doubles %Δd and adds to %ΔF.
Obtains 3.44%.
Obtains Δσ = 1.37 × 10⁶ Pa.

parts.prompt: Calculate the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in σ.
Hence state the absolute uncertainty Δσ in pascals.

Adds atmospheric pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa to Δp.
p_abs = 3.33 × 10⁵ Pa.
Uses F = p_abs A.

Determine the total absolute pressure acting at this depth.

items.stem: A heavy hinged trapdoor is held horizontal by an angled cable attached to its outer edge.
items.workedSolution: (a) product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force. (b) measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules. Core principle: perpendicular distance to the line of action is essential for a moment.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to perpendicular distance to the line of action is essential for a moment.
States primary causal step: measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (distance must be the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force).

parts.expectedAnswer: product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force.
workingSteps: Establish the core NCUK mark point: product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force.
Anchor concept: perpendicular distance to the line of action is essential for a moment.

parts.expectedAnswer: measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules.
workingSteps: Develop the causal explanation clearly without algebraic shortcuts: measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules.

items.stem: A geophysics technician machines a cubic basaltic core specimen whose mass is 4300 g ± 2.5 g and whose edge dimension measures 8 cm ± 0.08 cm.

markScheme.criterion: Converts mass to kg (× 10⁻³) and cubes converted side length (× 10⁻⁶ m³).
Obtains ρ = 8.40 × 10³ kg m⁻³.
Sums percentage uncertainty in mass with three times the percentage uncertainty in side length.
Obtains 3.06%.
Multiplies nominal density by fractional uncertainty to obtain Δρ = 257 kg m⁻³.

parts.prompt: Calculate the nominal density ρ of the cubic specimen in coherent SI units (kg m⁻³).
workingSteps: Convert inputs to SI base units: m = 4300 × 10⁻³ = 4.3 kg, L = 8 × 10⁻² = 0.08 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the percentage uncertainty in the calculated density.
Hence state the absolute uncertainty Δρ in kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Heating a sealed fluid changes the microscopic energies of its constituent particles.
items.workedSolution: (a) sum of random distribution of kinetic energies of all molecules in the system. (b) plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that sum of random distribution of kinetic energies of all molecules in the system.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules.

parts.prompt: State the first microscopic energy component included in internal energy. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: sum of random distribution of kinetic energies of all molecules in the system.
workingSteps: Identify the primary physical statement: sum of random distribution of kinetic energies of all molecules in the system.

parts.prompt: State the second microscopic energy component included in internal energy. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules.
workingSteps: Link the physical principle (internal energy combines microscopic random kinetic energy and molecular potential energy) to the required condition or mechanism: plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules.

items.stem: A fixed mass of ideal gas is sealed inside a rigid stainless-steel container and warmed steadily in an oven.
items.workedSolution: (a) raising temperature increases mean molecular kinetic energy and average molecular speed. (b) faster molecules produce larger momentum change per wall collision and higher collision frequency raising average force per unit area. Core principle: kinetic pressure arises from rate of momentum transfer to container walls rather than circular appeal to gas equations.

markScheme.criterion: States accurately that raising temperature increases mean molecular kinetic energy and average molecular speed.
First causal step: raising temperature increases mean molecular kinetic energy and average molecular speed.
Intermediate physical mechanism: molecules undergo a greater change in momentum during each elastic wall collision and strike the walls more frequently.
Final physical conclusion: by Newton second law the greater rate of change of momentum produces a larger average force over the fixed wall area raising pressure.

parts.prompt: State how raising temperature alters the mean kinetic energy and average speed of the gas molecules. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: raising temperature increases mean molecular kinetic energy and average molecular speed.
workingSteps: Establish the core NCUK mark point: raising temperature increases mean molecular kinetic energy and average molecular speed.
Anchor concept: kinetic pressure arises from rate of momentum transfer to container walls rather than circular appeal to gas equations.

parts.prompt: Without citing the ideal gas equation, explain using molecular collisions and Newton's second law why the pressure on the container walls increases. [3]
parts.expectedAnswer: faster molecules produce larger momentum change per wall collision and higher collision frequency raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Develop the causal explanation clearly without algebraic shortcuts: faster molecules produce larger momentum change per wall collision and higher collision frequency raising average force per unit area.
Avoid the common error of offering a circular algebraic restatement of the ideal gas equation instead of molecular momentum transfer.

Obtains 84.0%.
Obtains E_wasted = 3.66 × 10⁵ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the useful mechanical energy delivered against drag over the interval.
Determine the percentage efficiency of the drivetrain.
Calculate the energy wasted as heat during the interval.

items.stem: Taking upward as positive and g = 9.8 m s⁻² (air resistance negligible), a microgravity drop-tower catapult launches a sensor capsule vertically upward at 15 m s⁻¹; telemetry is sampled at t = 1.8 s after launch. What is the vertical displacement of the object relative to the launch point at t = 1.8 s?
items.workedSolution: With upward positive, u = +15 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.8 m s⁻². Vertical displacement s = ut + ½at² = (15)(1.8) − 0.5(9.8)(1.8)² = 11.1 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses s = ut − ½gt² with g = 9.8 m s⁻² to obtain 11.1 m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses +g instead of −g when initial velocity is upward, adding ½gt² to ut.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 1/2 in the gravitational displacement term −½gt².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the motion as release from rest and omits the upward initial-velocity term ut.

items.stem: An airport cargo pallet of mass 20 kg rolls on negligible-friction rollers at 3 m s⁻¹ before a strap pulls it with constant force 120 N at 60° above the horizontal for 8 s. What is the horizontal speed at the end of the 8 s interval?
items.workedSolution: Horizontal component F_x = 120 cos(60°) = 60 N ⇒ a_x = 3 m s⁻². Final speed v = u + a_x t = 3 + (3)(8) = 27.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a_x = 3 m s⁻² via F cos 60° / m and obtains v = 27.0 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the vertical component F sin θ instead of F cos θ to compute horizontal acceleration.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies F/m directly without resolving the angled force vector horizontally.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the velocity change Δv = a_x t and forgets to add the initial speed u.

items.stem: The diagram shows a two-input five-gate comparator network with intermediate nodes D and E leading to final output Q.
items.workedSolution: (a) $Q = (\bar{A} \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})$ (not A and B or A and not B forming an EOR gate). (b) 2 rows of the 4-row truth table give $Q = 1$. (c) Equivalent to a single two-input EOR gate.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly expresses intermediate nodes D and E in terms of inputs.
Writes exact unsimplified Boolean expression for Q ($Q = (\bar{A} \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})$).
Correctly simplifies expression: not A and B or A and not B forming an EOR gate.
Evaluates all 4 input rows accurately.
States 2 rows give $Q = 1$.
Identifies equivalent single two-input EOR gate.

items.stem: A cylindrical manganin heating wire has diameter 0.300 mm, length 2.50 m, and resistivity 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. If the entire wire is melted down with no loss of metal and recast into a solid cube, what is the edge length of the cube?
items.workedSolution: Wire area A = πd²/4 = 7.069 × 10⁻⁸ m², so volume V = AL = 1.767 × 10⁻⁷ m³. For a solid cube of equal volume, edge s = ∛V = 5.612 × 10⁻³ m = 5.61 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 5.61 mm.

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Took the square root rather than the cube root of the volume.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π from the cylindrical wire volume.

items.stem: On a crash-attenuator sled track, a 0.25 kg buffer module travelling at +32 m s⁻¹ impacts an elastomeric stop for 10 ms and rebounds in the reverse direction at speed 20 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A high-resistance digital voltmeter connected across an open-circuit bench battery module reads 10.5 V. When a 12.0 Ω resistor is connected across the terminals, the voltmeter reading drops to 9.00 V. If the 12.0 Ω resistor is replaced by a 4.00 Ω resistor, what is the new terminal potential difference?
items.workedSolution: Open-circuit reading gives ε = 10.5 V. With R₁ = 12 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 0.7500 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 2.000 Ω. With R₂ = 4 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 7.000 V ≈ 7.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 2.00 Ω and computes V₂ = 7.00 V.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumed terminal potential difference stays unchanged when load resistance changes.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: During a bench test, a hydrogen electrolysis cell runs from a regulated 9.00 V DC source at a steady current of 1.25 A for 4 min.
items.workedSolution: (a) One coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second. (b) Q = It = 300.0 C, so N = Q/e = 1.875 × 10²¹ ≈ 1.88 × 10²¹ electrons. (c) W = QV = 2.700 × 10³ J ≈ 2.70 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: States that one coulomb is the charge passing a point when a steady current of one ampere flows for one second.
Converts time to 240 s, computes Q = It = 300.0 C, and divides by e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Correct electron count 1.88 × 10²¹.
Correct electrical work W = QV = 2.70 × 10³ J.

items.stem: A rectangular carbon-film resistor track of resistivity 2.50 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m measures 60 mm long, 1.2 mm wide, and 0.5 mm thick. Calculate its resistance between the two opposite 1.2 mm × 0.5 mm end faces.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area perpendicular to current is A = w × h = (1.2 × 10⁻³ m) × (0.5 × 10⁻³ m) = 6.000 × 10⁻⁷ m², and L = 60 × 10⁻³ m. Using R = ρL/A yields 2.50 Ω.

options.label: D

items.stem: A student plots current on the vertical axis against potential difference on the horizontal axis for both an ohmic wire and a filament lamp. Which statement about determining resistance from these graphs is correct?
items.workedSolution: With current on the vertical axis the linear gradient equals the reciprocal of resistance while non ohmic resistance uses coordinate ratio. Verified key statement: with current on the vertical axis the linear gradient equals the reciprocal of resistance while non ohmic resistance uses coordinate ratio.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that with current on the vertical axis the linear gradient equals the reciprocal of resistance while non ohmic resistance uses coordinate ratio.

options.label: A
options.text: Correctly interpreted, the straight line gradient equals resistance directly and the tangent gradient gives lamp resistance
options.distractorRationale: Commits both classic I–V traps: gradient is 1/R (not R), and curved static resistance is V/I (not tangent).

options.label: B
options.text: Correctly interpreted, a steeper ohmic line always indicates a larger electrical resistance
options.distractorRationale: When I is on the vertical axis, steeper slope means larger I/V, hence SMALLER resistance.

options.label: C
options.text: Correctly interpreted, with current on the vertical axis the linear gradient equals the reciprocal of resistance while non ohmic resistance uses coordinate ratio

options.label: D
options.text: Correctly interpreted, resistance of a filament lamp equals the area underneath the curve up to that voltage
options.distractorRationale: Area under an I–V curve does not equal resistance.

items.stem: A cylindrical fine silver filament conductor in a micro-balance suspension wire carries a steady conventional current of 0.480 A from left to right. The metal has a free-electron number density of 5.70 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, and conduction electrons drift at a mean speed of 8.55 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) A = 6.156 × 10⁻⁸ m² ≈ 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m². (b) d = 0.280 mm. (c) Because electrons are negatively charged, they drift opposite to conventional current (right to left).

markScheme.criterion: Correct rearrangement A = I / (nve) with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Correct cross-sectional area 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m² (4 s.f. 6.156 × 10⁻⁸ m²).
Substitutes area into d = √(4A / π).
Correct final value 0.280 mm.
States electrons drift opposite to conventional current (from right to left).

items.stem: Which option correctly states Kirchhoff's first law and the underlying conservation principle it expresses?
items.workedSolution: Kirchhoff's first law states that the sum of currents entering a junction equals sum leaving expressing conservation of charge. Verified key statement: sum of currents entering a junction equals sum leaving expressing conservation of charge.

items.stem: A metallic wire connects the positive and negative terminals of a dry cell.
items.workedSolution: (a) conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current. (b) electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.

parts.prompt: State the direction of free electron drift relative to conventional current. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.
workingSteps: Identify the primary physical statement: conduction electrons carry negative charge and drift opposite to conventional current.

parts.prompt: State which battery terminal conduction electrons drift toward through the external wire. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.
workingSteps: Link the physical principle (conventional current tracks positive charge flow so negative electrons move the opposite way) to the required condition or mechanism: electrons move from the negative terminal toward the positive terminal of the supply.

items.stem: Two trolleys approach each other head-on from opposite directions on a smooth track. Why must opposite velocity signs be assigned when applying conservation of linear momentum?
items.workedSolution: Momentum is a vector so opposite directions carry opposite signs when computing total momentum. Verified key statement: momentum is a vector so opposite directions carry opposite signs.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that momentum is a vector so opposite directions carry opposite signs.

options.label: A

options.distractorRationale: Momentum is a vector quantity, not a scalar.

options.label: B
options.text: Because kinetic energy is always negative for any object moving toward the left
options.distractorRationale: Kinetic energy is a non-negative scalar independent of direction.

options.label: C
options.text: Because mass changes sign whenever a trolley reverses its direction of travel
options.distractorRationale: Mass is always positive; velocity carries the directional sign.

options.label: D

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that decreasing external load resistance lowers total circuit resistance and increases current drawn from the cell.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that greater current produces a larger potential drop or lost volts across the internal resistance.

items.stem: A light-dependent resistor and a fixed resistor form a potential divider in an automatic lamp sensor.
items.workedSolution: (a) greater incident light intensity liberates more mobile charge carriers lowering resistance of the light dependent resistor. (b) total series resistance falls causing current in the divider chain to increase.

Awards credit for stating or explaining that total series resistance falls causing current in the divider chain to increase.

items.stem: An alternating potential difference produces the sinusoidal trace shown on a cathode-ray oscilloscope with time-base 2.0 ms div⁻¹ and Y-gain 1.5 V div⁻¹. One complete cycle occupies 4.0 horizontal divisions and the vertical peak-to-peak height is 5.2 divisions. Calculate the root-mean-square voltage of the signal.
items.workedSolution: Peak-to-peak voltage $V_{\mathrm{pp}} = 5.2 \times 1.5 = 7.80 V$. Peak voltage $V_0 = V_{\mathrm{pp}} / 2 = 3.90 V$. Therefore $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = V_0 / \sqrt{2} = 2.76 V$ (frequency $= 125 Hz$).

markScheme.criterion: Correctly computes $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = V_{\mathrm{pp}} / (2\sqrt{2}) = 2.76 V$.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Stops at peak voltage V₀ without dividing by √2.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reports the full peak-to-peak voltage instead of rms voltage.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides peak-to-peak voltage by √2 instead of 2√2.

items.stem: A micrometer screw gauge (0.5 mm pitch, 50 thimble divisions) measures a thin steel guitar string. The last visible main sleeve mark is 4.0 mm and thimble division 37 aligns with the datum line. Before measurement, the closed jaws gave a zero error of -0.03 mm. What is the corrected diameter?
items.workedSolution: Raw reading $= 4.0 + 37 \times 0.01 = 4.37$ mm. Subtracting the signed zero error (-0.03 mm) gives corrected diameter $= 4.37 - (-0.03) = 4.40$ mm (4.40 mm).

markScheme.criterion: Corrected micrometer reading $= 4.40$ mm (4.40 mm).

items.stem: An oceanographic CTD profiler records depth h = 24 m ± 0.3 m in a stratified layer of mean density ρ = 1250 kg m⁻³ ± 12 kg m⁻³ (take exact g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹).

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes into p = ρgh with g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.
Obtains p = 2.94 × 10⁵ Pa.
Adds percentage uncertainties in ρ and h.
Obtains 2.21%.
Obtains Δp = 6.50 × 10³ Pa.

parts.prompt: Calculate the hydrostatic gauge pressure p at depth h in pascals.
Calculate the percentage uncertainty in p.
Hence state the absolute uncertainty Δp in pascals.

items.stem: In a mooring-tether vibration experiment, wave speed follows the dimensionally homogeneous formula v = Tᵃ μᵇ (unit constant) for measured tension 180 N ± 1.2 N and linear density 6 g m⁻¹ ± 0.1 g m⁻¹. Deduce the exponents a and b by dimensional homogeneity and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Matching SI base units: [v] = m s⁻¹, [T] = kg m s⁻², [μ] = kg m⁻¹. For kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, −2a = −1 ⇒ a = 0.5 and b = −0.5, so v = √(T/μ). With μ = 6 × 10⁻³ = 0.006 kg m⁻¹, v = √(180 / 0.006) = 173 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a = 1/2, b = −1/2, converts μ to 0.006 kg m⁻¹, and obtains v = 173 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Deduces v = √(T/μ) correctly but forgets to convert μ from g m⁻¹ into kg m⁻¹ (off by √1000).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses a = 1, b = −1 (computing T/μ with units m² s⁻²) without taking the square root required by dimensional homogeneity.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the dimensional ratio to √(μ/T), yielding s m⁻¹ instead of m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In a rotary arm calibration facility, a test mass moves steadily at v = 12 m s⁻¹ ± 0.25 m s⁻¹ in a horizontal circle of radius r = 0.8 m ± 0.05 m (a = v² / r). What is the absolute uncertainty Δa in the centripetal acceleration?
items.workedSolution: Nominal acceleration a = v²/r = 12² / 0.8 = 180 m s⁻². Fractional uncertainty Δa/a = 2(0.25/12) + (0.05/0.8) = 0.104. Absolute uncertainty Δa = a(Δa/a) = 18.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Calculates a = v²/r and multiplies by 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) to obtain Δa = 18.8 m s⁻².

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to double Δv/v for the squared v² factor before multiplying by a.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts Δr/r instead of adding it when propagating uncertainty across a quotient.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes absolute uncertainties (Δv)² / Δr directly into the formula v² / r.

items.stem: A molybdenum furnace-hanger filament of circular diameter d = 0.5 mm ± 0.01 mm supports a tensile load of F = 60 N ± 1.5 N. What is the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = π(0.5 × 10⁻³)² / 4 = 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m². Tensile stress σ = F / A = 4F / (πd²) = 3.06 × 10⁸ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 in m² to obtain σ = 3.06 × 10⁸ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses A = πd² instead of A = πd²/4 (treating diameter d as if it were radius r, off by a factor of 4).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter in millimetres directly without converting d² from mm² to 10⁻⁶ m².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by circumference πd instead of cross-sectional area πd²/4.

items.stem: Consider a coastal marine-aquarium acrylic viewing floor panel, which has a flat horizontal surface of area 1.8 m² situated at a depth of 18 m beneath the open surface of seawater of density 1030 kg m⁻³. Take atmospheric pressure at the free surface as 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the hydrostatic pressure difference Δp due solely to the overlying liquid column?
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1030 × 9.81 × 18 = 1.819 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 1.82 × 10⁵ Pa. Absolute pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 1.819 × 10⁵ = 2.829 × 10⁵ Pa = 282.9 kPa ≈ 283 kPa. Total force F = p_abs A = 2.829 × 10⁵ × 1.8 = 5.092 × 10⁵ N ≈ 5.09 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 1.82 × 10⁵ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds atmospheric pressure even though only the hydrostatic difference Δp = ρgh was asked.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to include g = 9.81 m s⁻².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gauge force instead of gauge pressure.

items.stem: Both mechanical work and the moment of a force multiply force by distance, yet moments are never written in joules. Why is the unit newton metre retained for a moment?
items.workedSolution: Moment is measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules. Verified key statement: measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules.

options.label: A
options.text: Because a moment is a scalar energy transfer identical to heat supplied to a beam
options.distractorRationale: Moment is a turning effect, not an energy transfer.

options.label: B
options.text: Because a moment uses distance parallel to the force whereas work uses perpendicular distance
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the geometry: work uses parallel displacement whereas moment uses perpendicular lever arm.

options.label: C
options.text: Because newton metre has completely different SI base dimensions from the joule
options.distractorRationale: Both share dimensions kg m² s⁻², yet they represent physically distinct vector/scalar concepts.

options.label: D
options.text: Because a moment is measured in newton metres which is a turning effect rather than mechanical work in joules

items.stem: In a materials metrology audit, a machined titanium-aluminide reference cube records a mass of 1140 g ± 1.5 g on a digital balance and an edge length of 7.5 cm ± 0.06 cm using vernier callipers. What is the percentage uncertainty in the calculated density of the cube?
items.workedSolution: Since ρ = m L⁻³, Δρ / ρ = Δm / m + 3(ΔL / L) = (1.5/1140) + 3(0.06/7.5). Expressing as a percentage gives 2.53%.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Δρ/ρ = Δm/m + 3(ΔL/L) to obtain 2.53%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Adds the percentage uncertainty in edge length once instead of multiplying it by the power exponent 3 for L³.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts percentage uncertainties in the quotient m / L³ instead of adding worst-case contributions.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Cubes the percentage uncertainty in L rather than multiplying the fractional uncertainty by 3.

items.stem: How does the internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas differ from that of a real liquid?
items.workedSolution: Because intermolecular forces are negligible, for an ideal gas intermolecular potential energy is zero so internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature. Verified key statement: for an ideal gas intermolecular potential energy is zero so internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that for an ideal gas intermolecular potential energy is zero so internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature.

options.label: A
options.text: Specifically, an ideal gas has zero molecular kinetic energy so its internal energy is purely potential
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the ideal-gas assumption completely: ideal-gas molecules have kinetic energy and zero potential energy.

options.label: B
options.text: Specifically, internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on container volume and not on temperature
options.distractorRationale: Ideal-gas internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature (and number of moles).

options.label: C
options.text: Specifically, for an ideal gas intermolecular potential energy is zero so internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature

options.label: D
options.text: Specifically, an ideal gas stores extra elastic potential energy inside stretched intermolecular bonds
options.distractorRationale: Ideal-gas molecules exert negligible intermolecular forces except during brief collisions.

items.stem: An examiner awards zero credit to a student who explains rising gas pressure upon heating solely by stating that pressure is proportional to temperature from the gas law. What physical principle is missing?
items.workedSolution: Marks require microscopic Newton second law mechanics: kinetic pressure arises from rate of momentum transfer to container walls rather than circular appeal to gas equations. Verified key statement: kinetic pressure arises from rate of momentum transfer to container walls rather than circular appeal to gas equations.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that kinetic pressure arises from rate of momentum transfer to container walls rather than circular appeal to gas equations.

options.label: A
options.text: Examiners look for kinetic pressure arises from rate of momentum transfer to container walls rather than circular appeal to gas equations

options.label: B
options.text: Examiners look for thermal expansion of the rigid steel flask reducing internal gas density
options.distractorRationale: A rigid vessel has fixed volume; pressure increase comes from faster molecular impacts.

options.label: C
options.text: Examiners look for a calculation of molar mass using Avogadro constant instead of molecular collisions
options.distractorRationale: Qualitative kinetic explanations require collision momentum transfer, not a molar mass plug-in.

options.label: D
options.text: Examiners look for gravitational potential energy increase of molecules rising inside the cylinder
options.distractorRationale: Gravitational energy changes are negligible compared to molecular kinetic energy.

items.stem: An autonomous underground haulage shuttle moves along a horizontal drift at constant speed 108 km h⁻¹ against 2400 N of resistive force, consuming 96000 W electrically for 45 s. What is the percentage efficiency of the propulsion drivetrain?
items.workedSolution: At constant velocity, tractive force F = 2400 N and v = 108/3.6 = 30 m s⁻¹. Useful power P_out = Fv = 2400 × 30 = 72000 W. Efficiency η = (72000/96000) × 100% = 75.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Converts speed to 30 m s⁻¹, computes P_out = Fv = 72000 W, and obtains η = 75.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies drag force in N by speed in km h⁻¹ without dividing speed by 3.6 to obtain watts.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical power dissipated as heat rather than drivetrain efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by velocity (F/v) instead of multiplying P = Fv.

Obtains v = 14.8 m s⁻¹.
Substitutes into s = ut + ½at² or ½(u + v)t.
Obtains s = 67.2 m.
Obtains v_mean = 8.40 m s⁻¹.

Calculate the horizontal displacement during the interval.

items.stem: The five-gate three-input logic network shown evaluates $Q = ((A \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})) \cdot C$. Across all eight combinations of $(A, B, C)$, for how many rows is $Q = 1$?
items.workedSolution: Factorising gives $A(B + \bar{B}) \cdot C = A \cdot 1 \cdot C = A \cdot C$. This is HIGH for $(1, 0, 1)$ and $(1, 1, 1)$: exactly 2 rows.

markScheme.criterion: Exactly 2 rows give $Q = 1$.

items.stem: An ideal voltmeter placed directly across the terminals of a solar storage battery on open circuit reads 12.6 V. When a 18.0 Ω load resistor is connected across the battery, the voltmeter reading falls to 11.3 V. The first load is then removed and replaced by a 6.00 Ω load resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 0.630 A and substitutes into r = (ε − V₁) / I₁.

workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 11.34 / 18 = 0.6300 A.

workingSteps: New current I₂ = ε / (R₂ + r) = 12.6 / (6 + 2.000 Ω) = 1.575 A.

items.stem: On a vertical Hooke's-law stand, the pointer of a helical coil spring reads x₁ = 12 mm ± 0.5 mm when unloaded and x₂ = 57 mm ± 0.5 mm under a calibrated load F = 18 N ± 0.4 N. Using Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx₁ + Δx₂, what is the percentage uncertainty in the spring constant k = F / (x₂ − x₁)?
items.workedSolution: Extension e = x₂ − x₁ = 57 − 12 = 45 mm with absolute uncertainty Δe = Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 mm. Thus %Δk = (%ΔF) + (%Δe) = (0.4/18 + 1/45) × 100% = 4.44%.

markScheme.criterion: Finds e = 45 mm, Δe = 1 mm, and obtains %Δk = 4.44%.
