options.distractorRationale: Omits constant pressure and wrongly uses Celsius instead of absolute kelvin temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: It states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure volume is inversely proportional to kelvin temperature
options.distractorRationale: Heating an isobaric gas expands its volume directly, not inversely.

options.label: C
options.text: It states that for a fixed mass of ideal gas at constant pressure volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin

options.label: D
options.text: It states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature volume is directly proportional to pressure
options.distractorRationale: Confuses Charles's law with an inverted version of Boyle's law.

items.stem: An electric hydrofoil water-taxi cruises at constant velocity 54 km h⁻¹ against 1500 N of drag while its motor pack draws 26471 W for 60 s. How much thermal energy is wasted by the drivetrain during the 60 s interval?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates (P_in − Fv)t in SI units to obtain 2.38 × 10⁵ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Finds wasted power P_in − Fv in watts without multiplying by the duration in seconds.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates useful mechanical work Fvt rather than wasted energy.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses speed in km h⁻¹ directly inside Fv without converting to m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Taking upward as positive and g = 9.81 m s⁻² (air resistance negligible), a microgravity drop-tower catapult launches a sensor capsule vertically upward at 36 m s⁻¹; telemetry is sampled at t = 1.8 s after launch.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes u = +36 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻² into v = u + at.
Obtains v = 18.3 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½gt² with consistent signs.
Obtains s = 48.9 m.
Obtains v_avg = 27.2 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the signed vertical velocity at the stated time.
Calculate the vertical displacement relative to the launch point.
Determine the average vertical velocity over this time interval.

items.stem: A glaciology instrument sled of mass 12 kg glides along horizontal frictionless ice at initial speed 1.5 m s⁻¹ when a winch cable applies a constant tension of 18 N angled at 36.87° above the horizontal for 4 s (sled remains in contact with the ice).

markScheme.criterion: Uses F cos 36.87° / m = 1.2 m s⁻² and v = u + at.
Obtains v = 6.30 m s⁻¹.
Substitutes into s = ut + ½at² or ½(u + v)t.
Obtains s = 15.6 m.
Obtains v_mean = 3.90 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Resolve the cable force horizontally to find the acceleration and calculate the speed at the end of the interval.
Calculate the horizontal displacement during the interval.
State the mean horizontal velocity over the interval.

items.stem: The three-input safety interlock shown computes $Q = (A \cdot B) + \bar{C}$ across eight possible input states $(A, B, C)$. For how many of the eight rows in the truth table is the alarm output $Q = 1$?
items.workedSolution: $\bar{C} = 1$ covers 4 rows ($C = 0$). Among the $C = 1$ rows, only $(1, 1, 1)$ satisfies $A \cdot B = 1$. Total HIGH rows $= 4 + 1 = 5$.

markScheme.criterion: Alarm output is HIGH for 5 rows.

items.stem: A heating element is made from a uniform cylindrical fine kanthal element of diameter 0.180 mm, length 2.40 m, and resistivity 1.40 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. It is connected across a steady 60.0 V DC supply.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates A = πd²/4 = 2.54 × 10⁻⁸ m² and substitutes into R = ρL/A.
Correct resistance 132 Ω.
Correct power P = V²/R = 27.3 W.
Computes conserved volume V = AL = 6.11 × 10⁻⁸ m³ and sets s³ = V.
Correct cube edge length 3.94 mm.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical resistance of the wire.
Calculate the thermal power output of the heating element at 60.0 V.
The wire is later melted down without loss and cast into a solid cube. Calculate the edge length of the cube in mm.
workingSteps: Volume conserved: V = AL = 2.545 × 10⁻⁸ m² × 2.4 = 6.107 × 10⁻⁸ m³.

items.stem: A pneumatic forging tup of mass 0.12 kg strikes a hardened anvil face at +20 m s⁻¹ and rebounds upward at speed 14 m s⁻¹ (opposite sign) following a 25 ms impact. What is the magnitude of the average force exerted on the object during the 25 ms impact?
items.workedSolution: Taking incoming velocity as +20 m s⁻¹ and rebound velocity as −14 m s⁻¹, |Δp| = 0.12(20 + 14) = 4.08 N s. With Δt = 25 × 10⁻³ = 0.025 s, F_avg = |Δp| / Δt = 163 N.

markScheme.criterion: Computes |Δp| = m(u + v_reb) and divides by 0.025 s to obtain 163 N.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts speed magnitudes m(u − v_reb)/Δt instead of accounting for velocity reversal m(u + v_reb)/Δt.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides by contact time in milliseconds without converting ms to seconds (off by 10³).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the impulse magnitude |Δp| in N s and forgets to divide by contact time Δt.

items.stem: An ideal voltmeter placed directly across the terminals of a demonstration zinc-carbon pack on open circuit reads 5.00 V. When a 4.00 Ω load resistor is connected across the battery, the voltmeter reading falls to 4.00 V. The first load is then removed and replaced by a 9.00 Ω load resistor.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 1.00 A and substitutes into r = (ε − V₁) / I₁.
Correct internal resistance 1.00 Ω.
Uses V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) (or finds I₂ then I₂R₂).
Correct terminal potential difference 4.50 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the internal resistance of the battery.
workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 4 / 4 = 1.000 A.
Internal resistance r = (ε − V₁) / I₁ = (5 − 4) / 1.000 A = 1.000 Ω ≈ 1.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new terminal potential difference across the 9.00 Ω resistor.
workingSteps: New current I₂ = ε / (R₂ + r) = 5 / (9 + 1.000 Ω) = 0.5000 A.
Terminal pd V₂ = I₂ R₂ = 0.5000 A × 9 = 4.500 V ≈ 4.50 V.

items.stem: A rechargeable cell pack connected across a 9.00 V supply draws a constant current of 650 mA for 10 min. How many electrons pass a fixed cross-section of the connecting wire in this time?
items.workedSolution: Convert time t = 10 × 60 = 600 s and current I = 0.6500 A. Total charge Q = It = 390.0 C. Number of electrons N = Q / e = 390.0 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 2.438 × 10²¹ ≈ 2.44 × 10²¹.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 2.44 × 10²¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert time from minutes to seconds (factor of 60 error).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applied the wrong unit conversion factor for current or time.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied charge by e instead of dividing Q by e.

items.stem: In a seismometer suspension test, the lower fiducial mark sits at x₁ = 18 mm ± 0.5 mm unloaded and moves to x₂ = 118 mm ± 0.5 mm when force F = 18 N ± 0.8 N is suspended. What is the absolute uncertainty Δk in the spring constant expressed in N m⁻¹?
items.workedSolution: Extension e = (118 − 18) × 10⁻³ = 0.1 m with Δe = 2(0.5) × 10⁻³ = 0.001 m. Nominal k = 18 / 0.1 = 180 N m⁻¹. Fractional uncertainty Δk/k = 0.8/18 + 0.001/0.1 = 0.0544, so Δk = 9.80 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines Δe = 2Δx with ΔF/F + Δe/e to obtain Δk = 9.80 N m⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes only one reading uncertainty Δx instead of 2Δx when evaluating Δ(x₂ − x₁).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts Δx₂ − Δx₁ = 0 on the extension difference, ignoring ruler uncertainty completely.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves k in N mm⁻¹ instead of converting extension from millimetres to metres.

items.stem: An automated agricultural cable gantry drawing 1765 W hauls an implement at constant speed 5 m s⁻¹ for 25 s using a tether tension of 500 N inclined at 53.13° to the furrow. What is the percentage efficiency of the haulage system?
items.workedSolution: Useful mechanical power P_out = F v cos θ = 500 × 5 × cos(53.13°) = 1500 W. Efficiency η = (1500 / 1765) × 100% = 85.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates P_out = Fv cos 53.13° = 1500 W and obtains η = 85.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses Fv sin θ instead of the component parallel to velocity Fv cos θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses un-resolved product Fv without multiplying by cos θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input power wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

items.stem: A rectangular doped wafer strip has length 22 mm, width 0.5 mm, and height 0.25 mm. A potential difference of 4.00 V is applied across its two 0.5 mm × 0.25 mm end faces, where its resistance is measured to be 2.64 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates A = w × h = 1.25 × 10⁻⁷ m² and substitutes into R = ρL/A.
Correct value 1.50 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m.
Substitutes V and R into P = V² / R.
Correct power dissipated 6.06 W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the cross-sectional area perpendicular to current flow and hence determine the resistivity of the material.
Calculate the electrical power dissipated in the bar at this potential difference.
workingSteps: Use P = V² / R with V = 4.000 V and R = 2.640 Ω.

items.stem: A bicycle headlight bulb is rated "6 V, 15 W" and is operated continuously at its rated voltage for 12 min.

markScheme.criterion: Correct resistance 2.40 Ω.
Correct energy transferred 1.08 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the operating resistance of the component.
Calculate the electrical energy transferred in 12 min.

items.stem: An overhead railway phosphor-bronze contact wire sample of length 2.5 m and area 0.8 mm² stretches elastically by 1.875 mm when loaded with 144 N (uncertainties: ±2% in stress, ±4% in strain). What is the absolute uncertainty ΔE in the Young modulus in pascals?
items.workedSolution: E = σ / ε = 2.40 × 10¹¹ Pa. Total percentage uncertainty %ΔE = 2% + 4% = 6.00%. Absolute uncertainty ΔE = E × (%ΔE / 100%) = 1.44 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes E and multiplies by (2% + 4%) to obtain ΔE = 1.44 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts percentage uncertainties |%Δσ − %Δε| in the quotient E = σ / ε.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses 10⁻³ m² instead of 10⁻⁶ m² when converting area from mm² to m².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies percentage uncertainties instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: A student investigates the current against potential difference characteristic of a tungsten filament lamp from zero voltage up to normal operating brightness.
items.workedSolution: (a) drift progression is impeded more strongly so resistance increases and the current against voltage curve flattens toward the voltage axis. (b) higher temperature increases lattice ion vibration amplitude causing more frequent electron collisions and higher resistance. Core principle: larger lattice ion vibrations impede electron drift and raise metallic resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: drift progression is impeded more strongly so resistance increases and the current against voltage curve flattens toward the voltage axis.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to larger lattice ion vibrations impede electron drift and raise metallic resistance.
States primary causal step: higher temperature increases lattice ion vibration amplitude causing more frequent electron collisions and higher resistance.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (metal lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude so conduction electrons suffer more frequent collisions).

parts.prompt: Describe the shape of the current against potential difference sketch graph and explain how resistance changes along the curve. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: drift progression is impeded more strongly so resistance increases and the current against voltage curve flattens toward the voltage axis.
workingSteps: Establish the core NCUK mark point: drift progression is impeded more strongly so resistance increases and the current against voltage curve flattens toward the voltage axis.
Anchor concept: larger lattice ion vibrations impede electron drift and raise metallic resistance.

parts.prompt: Explain microscopically in terms of metal lattice ions and conduction electrons why the filament behaves non-ohmically. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: higher temperature increases lattice ion vibration amplitude causing more frequent electron collisions and higher resistance.
workingSteps: Develop the causal explanation clearly without algebraic shortcuts: higher temperature increases lattice ion vibration amplitude causing more frequent electron collisions and higher resistance.
Avoid the common error of attributing rising lamp resistance to a loss of free electrons inside the metal wire.

items.stem: In a laboratory rheostat lead, a uniform cylindrical copper-tin bronze wire of diameter 0.900 mm carries a steady current of 2.10 A. The free-electron number density in the copper-tin bronze is 7.20 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the mean drift speed of the conduction electrons.
items.workedSolution: Convert diameter to metres: d = 9.000 × 10⁻⁴ m. Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = 6.362 × 10⁻⁷ m². Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives v = I / (nAe) = 2.865 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 2.87 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 2.87 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in A = πr² (four times too large an area).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied by 4 instead of dividing by 4 in A = πd²/4.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π when calculating the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: During a wet-runway braking certification, an autonomous tow tractor travelling at 72 km h⁻¹ decelerates uniformly at 3 m s⁻² over an interval of 3.5 s.

markScheme.criterion: Divides 72 by 3.6 to obtain u = 20 m s⁻¹ and applies v = u − |a|t.
Obtains v = 9.50 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½|a|t² or ½(u + v)t with SI units.
Obtains s = 51.6 m.
Obtains v_mean = 14.8 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Convert the initial speed into m s⁻¹ and calculate the speed at the end of the braking interval.
Calculate the distance travelled during the braking interval.
Determine the mean speed over this interval in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In a spacecraft shunt-regulator test, a ceramic load resistor rated at R = 16 Ω ± 0.4 Ω operates with terminal p.d. V = 36 V ± 0.6 V. What is the percentage uncertainty in the electrical power dissipated P = V² / R?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2(%ΔV) + (%ΔR) = 5.83%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the exponent factor 2 on %ΔV for the squared V² term.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts %ΔR from 2(%ΔV) because R is in the denominator.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the percentage uncertainties instead of adding them.

items.stem: A solid billet of oxygen-free copper with mass 3.2 kg and density 8930 kg m⁻³ is drawn without material loss into a uniform cylindrical wire of diameter 0.8 mm (or alternatively melted and cast into a solid cube). What is the total length of the drawn cylindrical wire in m?
items.workedSolution: Volume V = m / ρ = 3.2 / 8930 = 3.583 × 10⁻⁴ m³ (358.3 cm³). Wire cross-sectional area A = π(d/2)² = 5.027 × 10⁻⁷ m² ⇒ L = V / A = 712.9 m ≈ 713 m. Recast cube edge s = ∛V = 7.103 cm ≈ 7.10 cm.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value = 713 m.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses diameter d instead of radius d/2 in A = πr², giving one quarter of the true length.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits π from the circular cross-sectional area.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies mm → m only once instead of squaring 10⁻³ for area.

items.stem: A mine-shaft skip winch drawing 3832 W lifts an ore cage of mass 500 kg at constant velocity through a vertical height of 10 m in 16 s (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the percentage efficiency of the lifting system?
items.workedSolution: Useful gravitational potential energy ΔE_p = mgh = 500 × 9.81 × 10 = 4.91 × 10⁴ J. Input electrical energy E_in = 3832 × 16 = 61312 J. Efficiency η = (ΔE_p / E_in) × 100% = 80.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgh / (P_in t) × 100% with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 80.0%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits gravitational field strength g when computing gravitational potential energy mgh.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input energy wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides useful energy mgh in joules directly by input power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

items.stem: To cast a watchmaking gear-wheel ingot of rose gold-copper alloy with total mass 2.4 kg, a metallurgist melts together 75% gold (density 19.3 g cm⁻³) and 25% copper (density 8.93 g cm⁻³) by mass. Assume that the total volume of the alloy equals the sum of the constituent volumes.
items.workedSolution: (a) Density is mass per unit volume of a material. (b) V₁ + V₂ = 160.5 cm³ ≈ 160 cm³. (c) ρ = m / V = 1.496 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.50 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Defines density as mass per unit volume.
Finds both constituent masses and sums V₁ = m₁/ρ₁ and V₂ = m₂/ρ₂.
Total volume = 160 cm³.
Converts cm³ to m³ (× 10⁻⁶) and divides total mass by total volume.
Alloy density = 1.50 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³.

parts.prompt: Define the density of a substance.
parts.expectedAnswer: Density is defined as mass per unit volume of a material.
workingSteps: State that density is mass divided by volume.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total volume of the cast alloy sample in cm³.
Hence calculate the overall density of the alloy in kg m⁻³.

items.stem: In a process-engineering calibration, 2 kg of glycerol (c = 2400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) warms by 30 K when heated for 80 s by a 2118 W resistive element. What percentage of the electrical energy supplied is retained as internal thermal energy of the glycerol?
items.workedSolution: Q = mcΔT = 2 × 2400 × 30 = 144000 J and E_in = 2118 × 80 = 169440 J. Percentage retained η = (Q / E_in) × 100% = 85.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mcΔT / (P_in t) × 100% = 85.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical energy lost to the surroundings instead of the percentage retained.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides Q = mcΔT in joules directly by heater power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits sample mass m from Q = mcΔT.

items.stem: A uniform block of seasoned oak timber (density 560 kg m⁻³) of mass 6 kg floats freely at rest in calm freshwater of density 1000 kg m⁻³ (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What percentage of the block's total volume lies submerged below the surface?
items.workedSolution: Floating balance: ρ_fluid V_sub g = ρ_obj V g ⇒ V_sub / V = ρ_obj / ρ_fluid = 560 / 1000 = 0.5600 = 56.00% ≈ 56.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Submerged percentage = 56.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the density ratio ρ_fluid / ρ_obj.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Halves the Archimedes density ratio.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage protruding above the waterline rather than submerged.

items.stem: Repeated stopwatch measurements of a pendulum period are scattered evenly above and below the true value as shown on the target plot. Which experimental action specifically reduces the effect of this type of error?
items.workedSolution: Unpredictable scatter about the true value is random error, which is reduced by taking repeat measurements, discarding anomalies, and calculating the mean. Therefore option B is correct: repeat measurements discard anomalies and calculate the mean.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: repeat measurements discard anomalies and calculate the mean.

items.stem: An ultrasonic magnetostrictive wire waveguide operates under axial tension T = 64 N ± 4 N with linear mass density μ = 8 g m⁻¹ ± 0.08 g m⁻¹; dimensional homogeneity fixes the exponents in v = Tᵃ μᵇ (unit prefactor). What is the percentage uncertainty in the wave speed v deduced from dimensional homogeneity?
items.workedSolution: Dimensional homogeneity gives v = T^(1/2) μ^(−1/2). Hence %Δv = ½(%ΔT) + ½(%Δμ) = 0.5(4/64 + 0.08/8) × 100% = 3.62%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses exponents |1/2| and |−1/2| to obtain %Δv = 3.62%.

items.stem: In a rotary arm calibration facility, a test mass moves steadily at v = 16 m s⁻¹ ± 0.2 m s⁻¹ in a horizontal circle of radius r = 0.5 m ± 0.03 m (a = v² / r). What is the percentage uncertainty in the calculated centripetal acceleration a?

items.stem: Consider a geothermal brine-holding cistern floor, which has a flat horizontal surface of area 3 m² situated at a depth of 16.5 m beneath the open surface of concentrated brine of density 1140 kg m⁻³. markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 286 kPa.

workingSteps: Load current I₁ = V₁ / R₁ = 7.5 / 10 = 0.7500 A.
Internal resistance r = (ε − V₁) / I₁ = (9 − 7.5) / 0.7500 A = 2.000 Ω ≈ 2.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new terminal potential difference across the 4.00 Ω resistor.
workingSteps: New current I₂ = ε / (R₂ + r) = 9 / (4 + 2.000 Ω) = 1.500 A.
Terminal pd V₂ = I₂ R₂ = 1.500 A × 4 = 6.000 V ≈ 6.00 V.

items.stem: An optical sensor module connected across a 5.00 V supply draws a constant current of 85 mA for 6 min. How many electrons pass a fixed cross-section of the connecting wire in this time?
items.workedSolution: Convert time t = 6 × 60 = 360 s and current I = 0.08500 A. Total charge Q = It = 30.60 C. Number of electrons N = Q / e = 30.60 C / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 1.913 × 10²⁰ ≈ 1.91 × 10²⁰.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 1.91 × 10²⁰.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert time from minutes to seconds (factor of 60 error).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applied the wrong unit conversion factor for current or time.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied charge by e instead of dividing Q by e.

items.stem: While characterizing an actuator return spring, students note scale readings x₁ = 22 mm ± 0.8 mm and x₂ = 82 mm ± 0.8 mm for an applied load of 36 N ± 0.5 N. What is the absolute uncertainty Δk in the spring constant expressed in N m⁻¹?
items.workedSolution: Extension e = (82 − 22) × 10⁻³ = 0.06 m with Δe = 2(0.8) × 10⁻³ = 0.0016 m. Nominal k = 36 / 0.06 = 600 N m⁻¹. Fractional uncertainty Δk/k = 0.5/36 + 0.0016/0.06 = 0.0406, so Δk = 24.3 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines Δe = 2Δx with ΔF/F + Δe/e to obtain Δk = 24.3 N m⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes only one reading uncertainty Δx instead of 2Δx when evaluating Δ(x₂ − x₁).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts Δx₂ − Δx₁ = 0 on the extension difference, ignoring ruler uncertainty completely.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Leaves k in N mm⁻¹ instead of converting extension from millimetres to metres.

items.stem: A ski-area surface tow motor draws 1059 W from the supply while pulling a maintenance sled along a level flat at constant velocity 2.5 m s⁻¹ over 50 s with rope tension 600 N at 53.13° to the travel direction. How much energy is wasted to the surroundings over the 50 s interval?
items.workedSolution: Useful power P_out = Fv cos(53.13°) = 900 W. Wasted power = 1059 − 900 = 159 W. Over 50 s, E_wasted = (159)(50) = 7.95 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts Fv cos 53.13° from 1059 W and multiplies by 50 s to get 7.95 × 10³ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes wasted power in watts (P_in − P_out) and forgets to multiply by the time interval.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the useful mechanical work done Fvt cos θ instead of the wasted energy.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to resolve cable tension by cos θ before subtracting from input power.

items.stem: A rectangular rectangular graphite block of resistivity 4.50 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m has length 50 mm, width 1.2 mm, and height 0.8 mm. A steady potential difference of 12.0 V is applied across its opposite 1.2 mm × 0.8 mm end faces.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates A = w × h = 9.60 × 10⁻⁷ m² and substitutes into R = ρL/A.
Correct value 2.34 Ω.
Substitutes V and R into P = V² / R.
Correct power dissipated 61.4 W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the cross-sectional area perpendicular to current flow and hence determine the resistance of the bar.
Calculate the electrical power dissipated in the bar at this potential difference.
workingSteps: Use P = V² / R with V = 12.00 V and R = 2.344 Ω.

items.stem: A stage projector lamp carries the rating "24 V, 150 W". What steady current does it draw when operated at its rated voltage?
items.workedSolution: Using P = IV gives I = P / V = 150 / 24 = 6.250 A ≈ 6.25 A.

markScheme.criterion: Applies electrical power rating equations to obtain 6.25 A.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divided V by P instead of P by V.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculated working resistance R = V²/P instead of current I = P/V.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied power by voltage instead of dividing.

items.stem: On an acoustic string tensile bench, a brass wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 mm² extends elastically by 1.5 mm under a load of 216 N (stress ±2%, strain ±3%). What is the Young modulus E of the wire in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Tensile stress σ = F / A = 216 / (1.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.44 × 10⁸ Pa. Tensile strain ε = ΔL / L = (1.5 × 10⁻³) / 2 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁴. Young modulus E = σ / ε = 1.92 × 10¹¹ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates σ = F/A and ε = ΔL/L in SI units to obtain E = 1.92 × 10¹¹ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Converts mm² to m² using 10⁻³ instead of (10⁻³)² = 10⁻⁶, underestimating stress and Young modulus by 10³.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets both mm² → 10⁻⁶ m² and mm → 10⁻³ m unit prefix powers properly.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies tensile stress by tensile strain (σ × ε) instead of dividing σ / ε.

items.stem: A student analyses experimental readings obtained from a non-ohmic filament bulb.
items.workedSolution: (a) potential difference across the component divided by the current through it. (b) evaluated from the coordinate ratio rather than the reciprocal of the tangent gradient on a curved graph.

markScheme.criterion: Awards credit for stating that potential difference across the component divided by the current through it.
Awards credit for stating or explaining that evaluated from the coordinate ratio rather than the reciprocal of the tangent gradient on a curved graph.

parts.prompt: Define the electrical resistance of a component. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: potential difference across the component divided by the current through it.
workingSteps: Identify the primary physical statement: potential difference across the component divided by the current through it.

parts.prompt: State how static resistance at a point is obtained from a curved current–voltage graph. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: evaluated from the coordinate ratio rather than the reciprocal of the tangent gradient on a curved graph.
workingSteps: Link the physical principle (resistance is defined by the direct ratio of voltage to current) to the required condition or mechanism: evaluated from the coordinate ratio rather than the reciprocal of the tangent gradient on a curved graph.

items.stem: A cylindrical gold bond wire wire in a cryogenic sensor lead has a free-electron number density of 5.90 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ and carries a steady current of 0.650 A. Given that the mean electron drift speed is 7.16 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹, what is the diameter of the wire?
items.workedSolution: Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the cross-sectional area is A = I / (nve) = 0.6500 A / (5.900 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ × 7.160 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 9.617 × 10⁻⁸ m². Since A = πd²/4, d = √(4A/π) = 3.499 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.350 mm.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 0.350 mm.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reported the wire radius r = √(A/π) instead of the diameter d = 2r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Used A = πd² rather than A = πd²/4 when solving for diameter.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted the factor of π in the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: On a straight proving ground, a battery-electric prototype car travelling at 126 km h⁻¹ brakes with constant deceleration 2 m s⁻² over 4 s.

markScheme.criterion: Divides 126 by 3.6 to obtain u = 35 m s⁻¹ and applies v = u − |a|t.
Obtains v = 27.0 m s⁻¹.
Uses s = ut − ½|a|t² or ½(u + v)t with SI units.
Obtains s = 124 m.
Obtains v_mean = 31.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Convert the initial speed into m s⁻¹ and calculate the speed at the end of the braking interval.
Calculate the distance travelled during the braking interval.
Determine the mean speed over this interval in m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In a dynamic-braking resistor verification, R = 8 Ω ± 0.4 Ω is subjected to steady DC potential difference V = 24 V ± 0.4 V. What is the absolute uncertainty ΔP in the dissipated electrical power in watts?
items.workedSolution: Nominal power P = V² / R = 24² / 8 = 72.0 W. Fractional uncertainty ΔP/P = 2(0.4/24) + (0.4/8) = 0.0833, giving ΔP = 6.00 W.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates P = V²/R and multiplies by 2(ΔV/V) + (ΔR/R) to obtain 6.00 W.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses ΔV/V + ΔR/R without doubling ΔV/V for V².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts ΔR/R from 2(ΔV/V) in the quotient V²/R.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates (ΔV)² / ΔR directly instead of propagating fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: In a mechanical workshop, a hydraulic-valve annular seal ring is turned from solid aircraft aluminium of density 2700 kg m⁻³. It has outer diameter 36 mm, concentric central bore diameter 22 mm, and axial thickness 24 mm. What is the mass of this annular component in grams?
items.workedSolution: Outer radius R = 18 mm = 0.01800 m; inner radius r = 11 mm = 0.01100 m; thickness h = 0.02400 m. Volume V = π(R² − r²)h = 1.531 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (15.31 cm³). Mass m = ρ V = 0.04133 kg = 41.33 g ≈ 41.3 g.

markScheme.criterion: Correct mass = 41.3 g.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses outer and inner diameters instead of radii in π(R² − r²), inflating area by 4×.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes π(R − r)² instead of π(R² − r²).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the washer as a solid cylinder and omits the central hole.

items.stem: A borehole submersible pump drawing 7664 W raises 600 kg of brine through a vertical pipe of height 20 m in 24 s at steady speed; take g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the percentage efficiency of the lifting system?
items.workedSolution: Useful gravitational potential energy ΔE_p = mgh = 600 × 9.81 × 20 = 1.18 × 10⁵ J. Input electrical energy E_in = 7664 × 24 = 183936 J. Efficiency η = (ΔE_p / E_in) × 100% = 64.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mgh / (P_in t) × 100% with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 64.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits gravitational field strength g when computing gravitational potential energy mgh.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input energy wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides useful energy mgh in joules directly by input power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

items.stem: A rectangular cuboid ingot for an acoustic-bell bronze casting is machined from aerospace al-cu alloy measuring 8 cm × 3 cm × 3.5 cm. The alloy is composed of 50% copper (density 8930 kg m⁻³) and 50% aluminium (density 2700 kg m⁻³) by volume.
items.workedSolution: (a) Density is mass per unit volume of a material. (b) ρ = 5815 kg m⁻³ ≈ 5.82e+3 kg m⁻³. (c) V = 8.400 × 10⁻⁵ m³, so m = 0.4885 kg ≈ 0.488 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Defines density as mass per unit volume.
Uses volume-weighted average ρ = f₁ρ₁ + f₂ρ₂.
ρ = 5.82e+3 kg m⁻³.
Converts cuboid volume from cm³ to m³ (× 10⁻⁶) and multiplies by ρ.

parts.prompt: State the definition of density.
parts.expectedAnswer: Density is mass per unit volume of a material.
workingSteps: State density equals mass per unit volume.

parts.prompt: Calculate the overall density of this volume-mixed alloy in kg m⁻³.
Calculate the total mass of the cuboid ingot in kg.

items.stem: In an industrial thermal-bath check, 0.6 kg of copper calorimetry block (specific heat capacity 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated for 150 s by an electrical element drawing 64 W, increasing the temperature by 25 K. How much thermal energy is lost to the surroundings during the 150 s heating period?
items.workedSolution: Electrical energy supplied E_in = P_in t = 64 × 150 = 9600 J. Thermal energy retained by sample Q = mcΔT = 0.6 × 390 × 25 = 5850 J. Energy lost to surroundings = E_in − Q = 3.75 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mcΔT (5850 J) from P_in t (9600 J) to obtain 3.75 × 10³ J.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the thermal energy absorbed by the sample Q = mcΔT rather than the heat lost to the surroundings.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the total electrical energy supplied P_in t instead of subtracting mcΔT.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the rate of heat loss in watts without multiplying by the heating time t.

items.stem: A solid solid copper ballast block (density 8930 kg m⁻³) of mass 18 kg is suspended from a calibrated spring balance and lowered until it is completely submerged in seawater of density 1025 kg m⁻³ without touching the tank floor (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the upward buoyancy force (upthrust) acting on the submerged block?
items.workedSolution: Block volume V = m / ρ_obj = 18 / 8930 = 2.016 × 10⁻³ m³. Upthrust F_B = ρ_fluid V g = 1025 × 2.016 × 10⁻³ × 9.81 = 20.27 N ≈ 20.3 N. Apparent weight W_app = m g − F_B = 176.6 − 20.27 = 156.3 N ≈ 156 N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct value = 20.3 N.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports apparent weight instead of upthrust.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes displaced mass in kg without multiplying by g = 9.81 m s⁻².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses object density instead of fluid density, recovering the object's own weight.

items.stem: Electrical resistance is defined by $R = V/I$, where potential difference $V = W/Q$. Which expression states the ohm solely in SI base units?
items.workedSolution: $V = W/Q$ gives $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$, and dividing by $I$ in $\mathrm{A}$ gives $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-2}}$. Therefore option C is correct: kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere squared.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere squared.

items.stem: A tensile testing machine plots tensile stress on the vertical axis against tensile strain on the horizontal axis for a steel rod. How is Young's modulus determined from the plot?
items.workedSolution: Young's modulus equals the gradient of the initial straight line region of a stress against strain graph. Verified key statement: equals the gradient of the initial straight line region of a stress against strain graph.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that equals the gradient of the initial straight line region of a stress against strain graph.

options.label: A
options.text: Young's modulus equals the gradient of the initial straight line region of a stress against strain graph

options.label: B
options.text: Young's modulus equals the total area enclosed beneath the stress against strain graph up to fracture
options.distractorRationale: Area under stress–strain gives strain energy per unit volume (toughness), not Young's modulus.

options.label: C
options.text: Young's modulus equals the reciprocal of the gradient of the linear region of the graph
options.distractorRationale: Gradient is stress divided by strain, which is directly Young's modulus (not its reciprocal).

options.label: D
options.text: Young's modulus equals the highest stress coordinate reached near necking
options.distractorRationale: Maximum stress coordinate is the ultimate tensile strength.

items.stem: In a desalination feed tower (take exact g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹), brine of density ρ = 1200 kg m⁻³ ± 20 kg m⁻³ stands at depth h = 45 m ± 0.3 m above the bottom port. What is the hydrostatic gauge pressure p = ρgh at this depth in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure p = ρgh = 1200 × 9.8 × 45 = 5.29 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates p = ρgh = 5.29 × 10⁵ Pa.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes ρh and omits gravitational field strength g.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reports the numerical value in kilopascals while labelling the unit as pascals.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides ρg by depth h instead of multiplying ρgh.

items.stem: On a structural stay-cable testbed, transverse pulse propagation speed is governed by the dimensionally homogeneous relation v = Tᵃ μᵇ (k = 1). A load cell reads T = 75 N ± 2 N for a strand rated at μ = 8 g m⁻¹ ± 0.2 g m⁻¹. Deduce the exponents a and b by dimensional homogeneity and calculate the wave speed v in m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Matching SI base units: [v] = m s⁻¹, [T] = kg m s⁻², [μ] = kg m⁻¹. For kgᵃ⁺ᵇ mᵃ⁻ᵇ s⁻²ᵃ = m¹ s⁻¹, −2a = −1 ⇒ a = 0.5 and b = −0.5, so v = √(T/μ). With μ = 8 × 10⁻³ = 0.008 kg m⁻¹, v = √(75 / 0.008) = 96.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a = 1/2, b = −1/2, converts μ to 0.008 kg m⁻¹, and obtains v = 96.8 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Deduces v = √(T/μ) correctly but forgets to convert μ from g m⁻¹ into kg m⁻¹ (off by √1000).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses a = 1, b = −1 (computing T/μ with units m² s⁻²) without taking the square root required by dimensional homogeneity.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the dimensional ratio to √(μ/T), yielding s m⁻¹ instead of m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Telemetry from an indoor velodrome timing loop logs a cyclist's speed as 24 m s⁻¹ ± 0.4 m s⁻¹ around a circular bend of radius 5 m ± 0.03 m to evaluate centripetal acceleration a = v² / r. What is the percentage uncertainty in the calculated centripetal acceleration a?
items.workedSolution: For a = v² / r, Δa/a = 2(Δv/v) + (Δr/r) = 2(0.4/24) + (0.03/5). Multiplying by 100% gives 3.93%.

markScheme.criterion: Uses %Δa = 2(%Δv) + (%Δr) to obtain 3.93%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 on the fractional uncertainty of v despite v being squared in v²/r.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the percentage uncertainty of r from 2(%Δv) because r is in the denominator.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the percentage uncertainties instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: An acoustic piano-wire gauge of diameter d = 1.5 mm ± 0.01 mm experiences an axial tension of F = 75 N ± 0.6 N. What is the tensile stress σ in the wire in pascals?
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = π(1.5 × 10⁻³)² / 4 = 1.77 × 10⁻⁶ m². Tensile stress σ = F / A = 4F / (πd²) = 4.24 × 10⁷ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = πd²/4 in m² to obtain σ = 4.24 × 10⁷ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses A = πd² instead of A = πd²/4 (treating diameter d as if it were radius r, off by a factor of 4).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter in millimetres directly without converting d² from mm² to 10⁻⁶ m².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by circumference πd instead of cross-sectional area πd²/4.

items.stem: Consider an offshore drilling diving-bell deck hatch, which has a flat horizontal surface of area 2 m² situated at a depth of 22.5 m beneath the open surface of seawater of density 1025 kg m⁻³. Take atmospheric pressure at the free surface as 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the hydrostatic pressure difference Δp due solely to the overlying liquid column?
items.workedSolution: Hydrostatic gauge pressure Δp = ρ g h = 1025 × 9.81 × 22.5 = 2.262 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 2.26 × 10⁵ Pa. Absolute pressure p_abs = p_atm + Δp = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 2.262 × 10⁵ = 3.272 × 10⁵ Pa = 327.2 kPa ≈ 327 kPa. Total force F = p_abs A = 3.272 × 10⁵ × 2 = 6.545 × 10⁵ N ≈ 6.54 × 10⁵ N.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 2.26 × 10⁵ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to include g = 9.81 m s⁻².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gauge force instead of gauge pressure.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds atmospheric pressure even though only the hydrostatic difference Δp = ρgh was asked.

items.stem: Which statement gives the complete NCUK definition of the moment of a force about a pivot?
items.workedSolution: The moment of a force is the product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force. Verified key statement: product of force and perpendicular distance from pivot to the line of action of the force.

items.stem: For a radiation-shielding verification test, a cubic alloy sample is weighed at 164 g ± 2.5 g while its side length is determined to be 4.5 cm ± 0.06 cm. What is the bulk density of the cube expressed in coherent SI base units (kg m⁻³)?
items.workedSolution: Convert to SI base units: m = 164 × 10⁻³ = 0.164 kg and L = 4.5 × 10⁻² = 0.045 m. Volume V = L³ = (0.045)³ m³. Bulk density ρ = m / L³ = 1.80 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Converts mass to kg and cubed edge length to m³ to obtain ρ = 1.80 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides mass in kilograms by a single edge length in metres instead of cubing the converted length.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Applies the centimetre prefix 10⁻² once rather than cubing it to (10⁻²)³ = 10⁻⁶ when converting cm³ to m³.

items.stem: Thermodynamic systems store energy microscopically across molecular kinetic and potential modes.
items.workedSolution: (a) sum of random kinetic energies and intermolecular potential energies of all molecules. (b) for an ideal gas intermolecular potential energy is zero so internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature. Core principle: internal energy combines microscopic random kinetic energy and molecular potential energy.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies key concept: sum of random kinetic energies and intermolecular potential energies of all molecules.
Includes exact NCUK precision linked to internal energy combines microscopic random kinetic energy and molecular potential energy.
States primary causal step: for an ideal gas intermolecular potential energy is zero so internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature.
Completes full physical linkage without misconception (plus the sum of intermolecular potential energies due to forces between molecules).

parts.prompt: Define the internal energy of a system. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: sum of random kinetic energies and intermolecular potential energies of all molecules.
workingSteps: Establish the core NCUK mark point: sum of random kinetic energies and intermolecular potential energies of all molecules.
Anchor concept: internal energy combines microscopic random kinetic energy and molecular potential energy.

parts.prompt: Explain how this simplifies for an ideal gas and what single macroscopic variable determines its internal energy. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: for an ideal gas intermolecular potential energy is zero so internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature.
workingSteps: Develop the causal explanation clearly without algebraic shortcuts: for an ideal gas intermolecular potential energy is zero so internal energy depends solely on absolute temperature.
Avoid the common error of counting bulk macroscopic kinetic energy of a moving container as internal energy.

items.stem: A student tests Boyle's law using pressure and volume measurements of trapped dry air at constant room temperature. Which plotted graph provides the clearest straight-line confirmation?
items.workedSolution: Since p is inversely proportional to V, plotting pressure against reciprocal volume produces a straight line through the origin. Verified key statement: plotting pressure against reciprocal volume produces a straight line through the origin.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that plotting pressure against reciprocal volume produces a straight line through the origin.

options.label: A
options.text: Confirmation is clearest because plotting pressure against volume produces a straight line through the origin
options.distractorRationale: Pressure against volume is a curved hyperbola, not a straight line.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirmation is clearest because plotting pressure against volume squared produces a horizontal straight line
options.distractorRationale: Since p V is constant, p vs V squared is curved rather than horizontal.

options.label: C
options.text: Confirmation is clearest because plotting volume against pressure squared passes through the origin
options.distractorRationale: Inversely proportional variables linearise against reciprocal, not square.

options.label: D
options.text: Confirmation is clearest because plotting pressure against reciprocal volume produces a straight line through the origin

items.stem: An electric hydrofoil water-taxi cruises at constant velocity 36 km h⁻¹ against 2400 N of drag while its motor pack draws 28571 W for 60 s. What is the percentage efficiency of the propulsion drivetrain?
items.workedSolution: At constant velocity, tractive force F = 2400 N and v = 36/3.6 = 10 m s⁻¹. Useful power P_out = Fv = 2400 × 10 = 24000 W. Efficiency η = (24000/28571) × 100% = 84.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Converts speed to 10 m s⁻¹, computes P_out = Fv = 24000 W, and obtains η = 84.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies drag force in N by speed in km h⁻¹ without dividing speed by 3.6 to obtain watts.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical power dissipated as heat rather than drivetrain efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides force by velocity (F/v) instead of multiplying P = Fv.

items.stem: In an evacuated vertical test tube, a steel ball is projected upward at +28 m s⁻¹ (upward positive, g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Photogates record the motion after 2.2 s. What is the vertical displacement of the object relative to the launch point at t = 2.2 s?
items.workedSolution: With upward positive, u = +28 m s⁻¹ and a = −9.81 m s⁻². Vertical displacement s = ut + ½at² = (28)(2.2) − 0.5(9.81)(2.2)² = 37.9 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses s = ut − ½gt² with g = 9.81 m s⁻² to obtain 37.9 m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses +g instead of −g when initial velocity is upward, adding ½gt² to ut.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Forgets the factor of 1/2 in the gravitational displacement term −½gt².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the motion as release from rest and omits the upward initial-velocity term ut.

items.stem: A glaciology instrument sled of mass 50 kg glides along horizontal frictionless ice at initial speed 1.5 m s⁻¹ when a winch cable applies a constant tension of 187.5 N angled at 36.87° above the horizontal for 8 s (sled remains in contact with the ice). What is the horizontal speed at the end of the 8 s interval?
items.workedSolution: Horizontal component F_x = 187.5 cos(36.87°) = 150 N ⇒ a_x = 3 m s⁻². Final speed v = u + a_x t = 1.5 + (3)(8) = 25.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds a_x = 3 m s⁻² via F cos 36.87° / m and obtains v = 25.5 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses the vertical component F sin θ instead of F cos θ to compute horizontal acceleration.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Applies F/m directly without resolving the angled force vector horizontally.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the velocity change Δv = a_x t and forgets to add the initial speed u.

items.stem: The five-gate logic circuit shown implements $Q = (\bar{A} \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})$ from two binary inputs A and B. Across all four rows of its complete two-input truth table, how many input combinations produce output $Q = 1$?
items.workedSolution: $Q = (\bar{A} \cdot B) + (A \cdot \bar{B})$ is HIGH for $(A, B) = (0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ only, giving 2 HIGH rows.

markScheme.criterion: Exactly 2 input combinations yield $Q = 1$.

items.stem: A cylindrical cupronickel wire of diameter 0.280 mm, length 2.00 m, and resistivity 3.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m is uniformly redrawn at constant volume so its new diameter is doubled (0.560 mm). What is the new electrical resistance of the wire?
items.workedSolution: Initial area A = πd²/4 = 6.158 × 10⁻⁸ m² and R = ρL/A = 12.34 Ω. Scaling diameter by factor k = 2 scales area by k² and length by 1/k² at constant volume, so R₂ = R / k⁴ = 0.7714 Ω ≈ 0.771 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies constant-volume geometry accurately to obtain 0.771 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Only scaled area by k² and forgot that constant volume also changes length by 1/k².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumed resistance varies inversely with diameter rather than diameter to the fourth power.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted the scaling factor k⁴ when computing the redrawn resistance.

items.stem: A pneumatic forging tup of mass 0.25 kg strikes a hardened anvil face at +24 m s⁻¹ and rebounds upward at speed 9 m s⁻¹ (opposite sign) following a 8 ms impact. What is the signed change in kinetic energy ΔE_k = E_k,f − E_k,i during the impact?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ½m(v² − u²) including negative sign to obtain -61.9 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes positive energy lost (E_k,i − E_k,f) instead of the signed change E_k,f − E_k,i.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates ½m(v − u)² instead of ½mv² − ½mu².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds the two kinetic energies because the velocity reversed sign, forgetting v² is always positive.

items.stem: A high-resistance digital voltmeter connected across an open-circuit portable lead-acid pack reads 12.0 V. When a 10.0 Ω resistor is connected across the terminals, the voltmeter reading drops to 10.0 V. If the 10.0 Ω resistor is replaced by a 6.00 Ω resistor, what is the new terminal potential difference?
items.workedSolution: Open-circuit reading gives ε = 12.0 V. With R₁ = 10 Ω, I₁ = V₁/R₁ = 1.000 A and r = (ε − V₁)/I₁ = 2.000 Ω. With R₂ = 6 Ω, V₂ = ε R₂ / (R₂ + r) = 9.000 V ≈ 9.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Finds internal resistance r = 2.00 Ω and computes V₂ = 9.00 V.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumed terminal potential difference stays unchanged when load resistance changes.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the lost volts Ir instead of the terminal potential difference IR₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Scaled lost volts proportionally to R₂ / R₁ rather than recalculating circuit current I₂.

items.stem: A laboratory heater coil operates at a steady potential difference of 24.0 V and draws a constant current of 1.85 A for 2.5 min. How much electrical work is transferred during this interval?
items.workedSolution: Convert time t = 2.5 × 60 = 150 s and current I = 1.850 A. Charge Q = It = 277.5 C. Electrical work W = QV = 6.660 × 10³ J ≈ 6.66 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Converts units accurately and obtains 6.66 × 10³ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Forgot to convert operating time from minutes into seconds.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omitted the mA-to-A prefix conversion (10³ error).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculated charge Q = It instead of electrical work W = QV.

items.stem: A precision dynamometer audit records pointer positions x₁ = 20 mm ± 0.5 mm (unloaded) and x₂ = 65 mm ± 0.5 mm under force F = 18 N ± 0.4 N. Using Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx₁ + Δx₂, what is the percentage uncertainty in the spring constant k = F / (x₂ − x₁)?
items.workedSolution: Extension e = x₂ − x₁ = 65 − 20 = 45 mm with absolute uncertainty Δe = Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 mm. Thus %Δk = (%ΔF) + (%Δe) = (0.4/18 + 1/45) × 100% = 4.44%.

markScheme.criterion: Finds e = 45 mm, Δe = 1 mm, and obtains %Δk = 4.44%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the uncertainty of a single ruler reading Δx rather than summing Δx₁ + Δx₂ = 2Δx for the difference x₂ − x₁.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes Δ(x₂ − x₁) = Δx − Δx = 0 by subtracting absolute uncertainties in a difference.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides 2Δx by the final reading x₂ instead of by the extension e = x₂ − x₁.

items.stem: In an industrial shipyard dock, an electric haulage drum drawing 1067 W moves a hull cradle steadily at 2 m s⁻¹ for 25 s via a cable exerting 500 N at 36.87° to the horizontal rail. What is the percentage efficiency of the haulage system?
items.workedSolution: Useful mechanical power P_out = F v cos θ = 500 × 2 × cos(36.87°) = 800 W. Efficiency η = (800 / 1067) × 100% = 75.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates P_out = Fv cos 36.87° = 800 W and obtains η = 75.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses Fv sin θ instead of the component parallel to velocity Fv cos θ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses un-resolved product Fv without multiplying by cos θ.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of input power wasted rather than the useful efficiency.

items.stem: A rectangular germanium sensing bar of resistivity 1.80 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m measures 30 mm long, 0.6 mm wide, and 0.3 mm thick. Calculate its resistance between the two opposite 0.6 mm × 0.3 mm end faces.
items.workedSolution: Cross-sectional area perpendicular to current is A = w × h = (0.6 × 10⁻³ m) × (0.3 × 10⁻³ m) = 1.800 × 10⁻⁷ m², and L = 30 × 10⁻³ m. Using R = ρL/A yields 3.00 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses A = w × h in m² and R = ρL/A to obtain 3.00 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used the wrong cross-sectional face for the current direction.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Failed to square the mm-to-m conversion factor for area.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverted A and L in the resistance equation.

items.stem: A microscope illuminator is labelled "6 V, 18 W". What is its working electrical resistance when operating at its rated potential difference?
items.workedSolution: Using P = V² / R gives R = V² / P = 6² / 18 = 2.000 Ω ≈ 2.00 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Applies electrical power rating equations to obtain 2.00 Ω.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverted R = V² / P as P / V².

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Used V / P instead of V² / P.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculated the rated current I = P / V rather than the resistance.

items.stem: On an acoustic string tensile bench, a brass wire of length 2.5 m and cross-sectional area 0.8 mm² extends elastically by 1.875 mm under a load of 168 N (stress ±2%, strain ±4%). What is the absolute uncertainty ΔE in the Young modulus in pascals?
items.workedSolution: E = σ / ε = 2.80 × 10¹¹ Pa. Total percentage uncertainty %ΔE = 2% + 4% = 6.00%. Absolute uncertainty ΔE = E × (%ΔE / 100%) = 1.68 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Computes E and multiplies by (2% + 4%) to obtain ΔE = 1.68 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts percentage uncertainties |%Δσ − %Δε| in the quotient E = σ / ε.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses 10⁻³ m² instead of 10⁻⁶ m² when converting area from mm² to m².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies percentage uncertainties instead of adding fractional uncertainties.

items.stem: As the potential difference across a tungsten filament lamp is increased from zero, its current–voltage graph curves toward the voltage axis. What is the microscopic reason for this non-ohmic behaviour?
items.workedSolution: In a metal filament, higher temperature increases lattice ion vibration amplitude causing more frequent electron collisions and higher resistance. Verified key statement: higher temperature increases lattice ion vibration amplitude causing more frequent electron collisions and higher resistance.

markScheme.criterion: Selects the accurate qualitative statement identifying that higher temperature increases lattice ion vibration amplitude causing more frequent electron collisions and higher resistance.

options.label: A
options.text: As current rises, higher temperature increases lattice ion vibration amplitude causing more frequent electron collisions and higher resistance

options.label: B
options.text: As current rises, heating reduces the number of free conduction electrons inside the tungsten wire
options.distractorRationale: In a metal the conduction electron density stays nearly constant; lattice vibrations cause the resistance rise.

options.label: C
options.text: As current rises, tungsten atoms shrink in size so conduction electrons drift more slowly
options.distractorRationale: Atoms do not shrink; lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude about their sites.

options.label: D
options.text: As current rises, the tungsten wire lengthens significantly while temperature stays constant
options.distractorRationale: Thermal expansion is tiny compared to the large temperature-driven increase in resistivity.

items.stem: In a battery bank interconnect, a uniform cylindrical electrolytic copper wire of diameter 1.40 mm carries a steady current of 4.20 A. The free-electron number density in the electrolytic copper is 8.40 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the mean drift speed of the conduction electrons.
items.workedSolution: Convert diameter to metres: d = 1.400 × 10⁻³ m. Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = 1.539 × 10⁻⁶ m². Using I = nAve with e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives v = I / (nAe) = 2.030 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 2.03 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies I = nAve and A = πd²/4 to obtain 2.03 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Used diameter instead of radius in A = πr² (four times too large an area).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplied by 4 instead of dividing by 4 in A = πd²/4.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omitted π when calculating the circular cross-sectional area.

items.stem: During a wet-runway braking certification, an autonomous tow tractor travelling at 72 km h⁻¹ decelerates uniformly at 2.4 m s⁻² over an interval of 4.5 s. What is the speed of the vehicle in m s⁻¹ at the end of the 4.5 s braking interval?

markScheme.criterion: Converts u to 20 m s⁻¹ and obtains v = 9.20 m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts |a|t in m s⁻¹ directly from u in km h⁻¹ without converting units.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Adds |a|t instead of subtracting |a|t during braking deceleration.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the average velocity ½(u + v) over the interval instead of the final velocity.

items.stem: A laboratory manganin standard resistor of resistance R = 16 Ω ± 0.2 Ω carries a steady potential difference of V = 36 V ± 0.3 V. What is the percentage uncertainty in the electrical power dissipated P = V² / R?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2(%ΔV) + (%ΔR) = 2.92%.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the exponent factor 2 on %ΔV for the squared V² term.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts %ΔR from 2(%ΔV) because R is in the denominator.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies the factor of 2 to %ΔR instead of %ΔV.

items.stem: A dense terrestrial dwarf planet surveyed by an orbital probe has mass 7.40 × 10²⁴ kg and mean diameter 13000 km. Model the body as a uniform sphere. What is its mean density in kg m⁻³?
items.workedSolution: Radius r = D / 2 = 6.500 × 10⁶ m. Volume V = (4/3)πr³ = 1.150 × 10²¹ m³. Mean density ρ = m / V = 6433 kg m⁻³ ≈ 6.43e+3 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Correct spherical density = 6.43e+3 kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides sphere volume incorrectly by a factor of 2.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 4/3 factor in the sphere volume formula.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes diameter D instead of radius D/2 into (4/3)πr³, producing an 8× too-small density.

items.stem: In a grain-silo elevator test (g = 9.81 m s⁻²), an electric drive consuming 4598 W lifts a 500 kg batch vertically through 15 m at constant speed in 20 s. How much energy is wasted during the 20 s lift?

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts mgh from P_in t to obtain 1.84 × 10⁴ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the gravitational potential energy gained mgh instead of wasted energy.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates wasted power in watts without multiplying by duration t.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Forgets to multiply mass and height by g when subtracting useful work from P_in t.

items.stem: To cast a metallurgical lab test ingot of rose gold-copper alloy with total mass 1.2 kg, a metallurgist melts together 70% gold (density 19.3 g cm⁻³) and 30% copper (density 8.93 g cm⁻³) by mass. Assume that the total volume of the alloy equals the sum of the constituent volumes. What is the overall density of the finished alloy in kg m⁻³?
items.workedSolution: Masses: m₁ = 0.8400 kg, m₂ = 0.3600 kg. Volumes: V₁ = m₁/ρ₁ = 4.352 × 10⁻⁵ m³, V₂ = m₂/ρ₂ = 4.031 × 10⁻⁵ m³. Total volume V = V₁ + V₂ = 8.384 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (83.84 cm³). Alloy density ρ = m / V = 1.2 / 8.384 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.431 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ ≈ 1.43 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³ (14.3 g cm⁻³).

markScheme.criterion: Correct harmonic-mean alloy density = 1.43 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses an incorrect geometric factor or lever-arm ratio.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the density in g cm⁻³ instead of converting to kg m⁻³.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies the arithmetic weighted mean w₁ρ₁ + w₂ρ₂, which is only valid for volume fractions.

items.stem: During a calorimetry practical, a 100 W cartridge heater operates continuously for 120 s in 0.5 kg of aluminium calorimetry block (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) and produces a temperature rise of 20 K. What percentage of the electrical energy supplied is retained as internal thermal energy of the aluminium calorimetry block?
items.workedSolution: Q = mcΔT = 0.5 × 900 × 20 = 9000 J and E_in = 100 × 120 = 12000 J. Percentage retained η = (Q / E_in) × 100% = 75.0%.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates mcΔT / (P_in t) × 100% = 75.0%.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the percentage of electrical energy lost to the surroundings instead of the percentage retained.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides Q = mcΔT in joules directly by heater power P_in in watts without dividing by time t.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits sample mass m from Q = mcΔT.

items.stem: A sample of industrial brine has density 1068 kg m⁻³ and contains 9% dissolved sodium chloride by mass. A desalination engineer wishes to extract 3 kg of pure solid salt by evaporating this liquid. What volume of industrial brine, in litres, must be evaporated?
items.workedSolution: Required solution mass m_sol = 3 / (9 / 100) = 33.33 kg. Volume V = m_sol / ρ = 33.33 / 1068 = 0.03121 m³ = 31.21 L ≈ 31.2 L.

markScheme.criterion: Correct solution volume = 31.2 L.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by the mass fraction instead of dividing by it.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the volume in m³ instead of converting to litres (× 1000).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Ignores the solute mass percentage completely.

items.stem: Photon energy is linked to frequency by $E = hf$. Which combination of coherent SI base units is equivalent to the unit of the Planck constant $h$?
items.workedSolution: Since $h = E/f = E T$, multiplying $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$ by $\mathrm{s}$ yields $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Therefore option D is correct: kilogram metre squared per second.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: kilogram metre squared per second.
